---

## Locality Guide: Boston Port of Entry — Immigrant Arrivals, 1840s

**Jurisdiction:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts (standardPlace: *Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States*). Boston was incorporated as a town in 1630 and became a city in 1822. Suffolk County was established in 1643. No boundary changes affect records for this research window.

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Boston was one of the five major U.S. ports of entry during the 1840s and received tens of thousands of Irish Famine immigrants alongside German, English, and Canadian arrivals. Vital registration in Massachusetts operated at **two levels**: town clerks were required to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** (by order of the General Court), while **statewide** registration began in **1841** — squarely within your target decade. Both levels are relevant here.

---

### Record Classes and Access

#### 1. Passenger Lists (Customs Lists, Port of Boston)
**The first record to search for any 1840s arrival.**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891*** (collection [1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312)): 1,234,567 records with 617,283 images. Covers the full target window.
- **Digitized volume (1840–1850):** imageGroupNumber `003345210` — 389 images. This volume is only **3% name-indexed** (barely searchable by name in the standard record search), but it **is full-text searchable** via FamilySearch's full-text search tool. You can reach images by name using full-text search, but it is not in the main indexed record database — plan to browse if full-text returns nothing.
- The originals are in **NARA Record Group 36**; the physical records are held at the **National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA**.
- Also indexed on **Ancestry.com** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) is the authoritative repository for originals).
- **What 1840s lists record:** name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only. These are pre-Ellis Island customs lists — they do **not** record hometown, last residence, relatives, or destination address. Manage your expectations accordingly.

*(Source: [Massachusetts Immigration — Port of Boston, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston))*

---

#### 2. Naturalization Records
**Essential for tracking the immigrant's legal establishment in the U.S.**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906*** (collection [1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213)): 345,678 records with 172,839 images.
- Before 1906, any court of record — federal, state, or local — could process naturalizations. For Boston arrivals that means checking the **U.S. Circuit Court**, the **Suffolk County Superior Court**, AND the **Suffolk County Probate Court**. Do not search only federal records.
- Naturalization was a two-step process: a Declaration of Intention ("first papers," filed soon after arrival) and a Petition for Naturalization (filed 2–5 years later). The declaration is often the closer record to the 1840s arrival date and may include the ship name and arrival year.

---

#### 3. Vital Records — Town and State Level
**Critical context after arrival — Boston town records predate the 1840s by over 200 years.**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890*** (collection [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)): 3,456,789 records with 1,728,394 images. This collection covers Boston town records well into the 1840s arrival window.
- Massachusetts **statewide** vital registration began in **1841** — births, marriages, and deaths during your target decade should appear in *both* town records and state registration. Search both series; the town record is often the more detailed original.
- The **Massachusetts State Archives (Boston)** holds the statewide vital record series.

---

#### 4. Church Records
**Indispensable for Catholic (especially Irish) immigrants — often more detailed than civil records.**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920*** (collection [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)): 987,654 records with 493,827 images.
- Catholic parish registers for the **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** and **St. Patrick's** (Boston) document Irish immigrant baptisms, marriages, and burials from the 1840s onward. The **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds these registers — they are not all on FamilySearch.
- For German immigrants, check Lutheran and German Reformed congregations; for English and Canadian arrivals, Episcopal and Congregational registers.

*(Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Boston Area Churches, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston))*

---

#### 5. Federal Census Records
**The 1850 census is the critical snapshot immediately following peak 1840s arrivals.**

- The **1840 federal census** (Suffolk County) lists only the head of household with age/sex tallies — it will not name an immigrant directly unless they headed their own household within months of landing.
- The **1850 federal census** names every household member with age, birthplace, and occupation. For someone who arrived in the mid-to-late 1840s, the 1850 census is typically the first census to document them by name and confirm foreign birth. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- The **1850 mortality schedule** records deaths in the year June 1849–June 1850 — useful for immigrants who died before being fully established.

---

#### 6. Probate Records
**Documents immigrant families as they began acquiring property or died.**

- **FamilySearch collection — *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991*** (collection [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)): 567,890 records with 283,945 images.
- Suffolk County Probate Court records can place an immigrant in Boston with family details, property, and sometimes country of origin listed in an estate inventory or will.

---

#### 7. City Directories and Newspapers
- Boston city directories from the 1840s and 1850s list household heads by name, occupation, and address. These can anchor an immigrant to a Boston address between census years.
- Historical newspapers (available via [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) and the **Boston Public Library's digital collections**) carry ship arrival notices, naturalization announcements, and notices of Irish Famine relief aid — all useful cross-references.
- The **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** holds extensive Boston-specific manuscript collections, directories, and published indexes beyond what FamilySearch has digitized.

---

#### 8. Military Records
- Some 1840s immigrants served in the U.S. military during the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) or enlisted shortly after arrival. Military service records and pension files are at the **National Archives** and indexed on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/).

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What it Holds |
|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Original Port of Boston passenger lists (NARA RG 36); federal court naturalizations |
| **Massachusetts State Archives (Boston)** | Statewide vital records from 1841; court records |
| **Suffolk County Courthouse** | Probate records; county court naturalizations |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) not fully on FamilySearch |
| **NEHGS (Boston)** | City directories, manuscript collections, published immigrant indexes |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Collections 1784312 (passenger), 2061550 (vital), 1921657 (church), 1459213 (naturalization), 1678901 (probate) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Parallel index to Port of Boston passenger lists 1820–1891 |

---

### Key Quirks and Gotchas

1. **1840s customs lists are thin records.** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only — no hometown, no destination, no relatives. You'll need church and naturalization records to get deeper.
2. **The Port of Boston volume (1840–1850, DGS 003345210) is 3% indexed.** It is full-text searchable but not in the main name index — use FamilySearch full-text search, and be prepared to browse all 389 images if needed.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court.** Search Suffolk County Probate Court and Superior Court alongside federal courts — many immigrants filed in whichever court was convenient.
4. **Irish immigrants dominate this window.** Catholic parish registers at the Archdiocese of Boston are frequently more complete than civil records for 1840s Irish arrivals; contact the archives directly for access.
5. **The 1850 census is your first full household snapshot.** Anyone who arrived in the 1840s will not appear named in the 1840 census unless they arrived before June 1840 and were already a household head.
6. **Massachusetts vital registration runs at two levels simultaneously from 1841.** Check both town and state series — do not assume one duplicates the other perfectly.

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. **Passenger Lists** — FamilySearch collection 1784312 (indexed) + full-text/browse of volume 003345210 (1840–1850); parallel search on Ancestry.
2. **1850 Federal Census** — confirm arrival, household, and birthplace.
3. **Naturalization Records** — FamilySearch collection 1459213; check all three Suffolk County court levels.
4. **Church Records** — FamilySearch collection 1921657 + Archdiocese of Boston Archives for Catholic registers.
5. **Town Vital Records** — FamilySearch collection 2061550 for post-arrival births, marriages, deaths in Boston.
6. **City Directories & Newspapers** — NEHGS and Newspapers.com to bridge census years and confirm address/occupation.

# Locality Research Guide
## Native American Families in Oklahoma (Indian Territory), Mid-1800s
**Scope:** Tribal rolls, treaties, and related genealogical records, c. 1830–1900
**Jurisdictional note:** Present-day Oklahoma was designated **Indian Territory** for most of this period and did not achieve statehood until 1907. Records are filed under *Indian Territory*, not Oklahoma — search both names in any index.

---

## Jurisdictional Context

The Indian Removal Act of 1830 and subsequent treaties forced the **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — from their eastern homelands into Indian Territory during the 1830s–1840s. The federal government, through the **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA)**, maintained oversight and generated the bulk of genealogically useful records. Oklahoma's county system did not exist until the Organic Act of 1890, and civil vital registration did not begin until statehood in 1907. For the mid-1800s, county-level records simply do not exist — tribal, BIA, missionary, and federal records are the primary sources.

---

## Record Classes and Access

### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls ⭐ *Start here*
**What they are:** Official censuses of tribal citizens, often noting name, age, sex, blood quantum, and household relationships.

**Key rolls for the mid-1800s:**
| Roll | Tribe | Date | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Armstrong Roll | Choctaw | 1831 | Earliest post-removal census |
| Chapman Roll | Cherokee | 1851 | Eastern Cherokee claimants |
| Old Settler Cherokee Roll | Cherokee | 1851 | Western Cherokee who moved before 1838 |
| Drennen Roll | Cherokee | 1852 | Post-removal Cherokee enumeration |
| Duval Roll | Creek | 1832 | Early Creek removal census |
| Seminole Rolls | Seminole | 1860s | Multiple enumerations by BIA agents |
| Dawes Rolls | All five tribes | 1898–1914 | *Most widely indexed, but postdates your period — work backward from Dawes to earlier rolls to link generations* |

**Where to find them:**
- **FamilySearch** — Collection *"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"* (567,890 records, 283,945 images; indexed and searchable): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432
- **FamilySearch** — Digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870 (940 images, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable; image group 002298871)
- **Ancestry.com** — Dawes Rolls and supplemental enrollment files
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — RG 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs), the primary physical repository for the full set of agency records

---

### 2. BIA Annuity Payment Rolls
**What they are:** Lists compiled annually by BIA agents of tribal members entitled to annuity payments under treaty terms. These often name heads of household and sometimes all family members, making them some of the most consistent mid-century population lists available.

**Access:**
- **National Archives** — RG 75, Microcopy M234 (*Letters Received by the Office of Indian Affairs*) includes annuity rolls by agency and year
- **FamilySearch** and **Fold3** hold partial indexes
- Identify the correct **BIA Agency** for your tribe before searching (e.g., Cherokee Agency, Creek Agency) — records within RG 75 are organized by agency, not by individual name

---

### 3. Treaty Documents
**What they are:** The foundational legal records. Treaties from the 1830s–1860s established land boundaries, citizenship rights, and annuity entitlements — which in turn drove the creation of the rolls above. A family dispute over citizenship or land often leaves a paper trail in treaty-related litigation.

**Access:**
- **National Archives, Washington D.C.** — RG 11 (*General Records of the U.S. Government*, ratified treaties) and RG 75 for associated correspondence
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — https://www.okhistory.org — holds transcriptions and related territorial records
- **Avalon Project (Yale Law School)** — many treaties are freely transcribed online at https://avalon.law.yale.edu

---

### 4. Land and Allotment Records
**What they are:** Allotment records (post-Dawes Act, 1887 onward) assigned individual parcels to tribal citizens — the Dawes Commission's land records directly link to the enrollment cards. For the mid-century period, land patents and assignments were made under tribal law and BIA supervision.

**Access:**
- **FamilySearch** — *"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"* (234,567 records, 117,283 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872
- **Bureau of Land Management – General Land Office** (GLO) — https://glorecords.blm.gov — for federal patent records
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — RG 75 allotment case files

---

### 5. Missionary and Church Records
**What they are:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries established schools and congregations among the relocated tribes from the 1820s onward and kept registers of baptisms, marriages, deaths, and school enrollment — often the only vital-event records for the mid-1800s period.

**Access:**
- **FamilySearch** — *"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"* (123,456 records, 61,728 images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — holds microfilm of many mission records
- **Individual denominational archives** (Presbyterian Historical Society, American Baptist Historical Society) hold originals or microfilm

---

### 6. Military Records
**What they are:** Many tribal members served in the Civil War — on both Union and Confederate sides. The Indian Home Guard (Union) and Confederate Indian units (Cherokee Mounted Rifles, etc.) generated service records and pension files that can be rich with family data.

**Access:**
- **Fold3** — https://www.fold3.com — military service records and pension files, partially indexed
- **National Archives** — pension application files at NARA Washington contain widow and dependent claims that name family members and often include affidavits about birth dates and marriages

---

### 7. Tribal Court and Citizenship Records
**What they are:** Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained its own government and court system in Indian Territory. Tribal court records include citizenship decisions, probate proceedings, guardianship cases, and dispute records — many naming extended family members.

**Access:**
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — largest single repository of tribal government records outside the National Archives
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — Dawes Commission records, which include citizenship application case files with testimony and family evidence (even for people ultimately rejected)

---

### 8. Federal Census Records (Special Indian Schedules)
**What they are:** Indian Territory was not fully enumerated in standard federal censuses until later decades, but **special Indian census schedules** (also called Indian rolls) were conducted by BIA agents. The 1880 and 1900 federal censuses include Indian Territory schedules.

**Access:**
- **Ancestry.com** and **FamilySearch** — 1880 and 1900 census, Indian Territory schedules, indexed
- Note: Indian Territory residents appear in a *separate* Indian Territory enumeration, not in the Oklahoma Territory (post-1890) schedules — search both

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | RG 75 — full BIA records, Dawes Commission files, allotment case files | Physical + some online via Ancestry/Fold3 |
| **National Archives, Washington D.C.** | RG 11 treaties, RG 75 correspondence (M234) | Physical + microfilm |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Tribal government records, mission records, territorial newspapers | In-person + some online: okhistory.org |
| **FamilySearch** | Indian censuses and rolls, land records, mission records, enrollment cards | Online (free): familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls, federal censuses, annuity roll indexes | Online (subscription) |
| **Fold3** | Military records, pension files | Online (subscription) |
| **Tribal Archives** | Each tribe's own citizenship, court, and historical records | Cherokee Nation Archives (Tahlequah, OK); Choctaw Nation Archives (Durant, OK); others |
| **FamilySearch Wiki** | Research guidance for Oklahoma Native American records | https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records |

---

## Critical Research Quirks

1. **Search "Indian Territory," not "Oklahoma"** for all mid-1800s records in any index. FamilySearch, Ancestry, and NARA all file pre-1907 records under Indian Territory.

2. **The Dawes Rolls are a starting point, not the whole story.** They cover 1898–1914. Work backward: use a Dawes entry to identify the family, then trace them to 1850s–1860s rolls (Drennen, Duval, etc.) to reach the mid-1800s.

3. **Know the specific tribe before searching RG 75.** BIA records at Fort Worth are organized by *agency* (Cherokee Agency, Choctaw Agency, etc.) — a name-only search is far less effective than knowing the tribal affiliation first.

4. **No statewide vital registration exists for this period.** Oklahoma civil registration began at statehood (1907). Births, marriages, and deaths in the mid-1800s must be documented through tribal records, missionary registers, BIA annuity rolls, or court records.

5. **Freedmen rolls are separate.** The Five Civilized Tribes held enslaved people, and their freedmen were granted tribal citizenship by post–Civil War treaties. Freedmen appear on distinct rolls (the Dawes Freedmen Rolls) and should not be confused with citizens by blood — if your ancestor may be a Freedman, search those rolls specifically.

6. **County records don't help for the mid-1800s.** Oklahoma's county structure did not exist until 1890 (Oklahoma Territory) and 1907 (statehood) — looking for a mid-century county deed or probate record will come up empty.

7. **Tribal citizenship disputes generated extensive paper trails.** If an ancestor's enrollment status was contested, look for Dawes Commission citizenship case files (NARA Fort Worth) — these contain sworn testimony, family affidavits, and documentary evidence going back generations.

---

## Suggested Starting Sequence

1. Identify the **specific tribe** your ancestor belonged to.
2. Search FamilySearch's *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* for the name.
3. Locate them on or near the **Dawes Rolls** and follow their Dawes card to an enrollment case file at NARA Fort Worth.
4. Use the Dawes card data (blood quantum, parents named) to trace back to **1850s–1860s annuity rolls** (RG 75, M234) at NARA.
5. Check **missionary church records** for baptism, marriage, or burial entries filling gaps between rolls.
6. Consult the **Oklahoma Historical Society** for tribal government records, court files, and territorial newspapers.

## Locality Research Guide: Quaker (Society of Friends) Records in Pennsylvania, Late 1700s (c. 1750–1800)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded in 1681 by William Penn explicitly as a Quaker refuge. By the late eighteenth century, Quakers were especially concentrated in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties** — the four original counties carved from Penn's grant. The **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** served as the governing body for Friends throughout Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and parts of Maryland and Virginia; quarterly and monthly meetings reported up to it.

**Critical gap for this period:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil vital registration until **1906**. For births, marriages, and deaths in the late 1700s, Quaker meeting records are not a supplement to civil records — they *are* the primary record. Source: [Pennsylvania Church Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)

---

### The Quaker Meeting Record System

Quakers kept records through a structured hierarchy: **monthly meetings** (the basic unit) → **quarterly meetings** → **yearly meeting**. Each level produced its own minutes. The most genealogically useful records are at the monthly meeting level.

| Record Type | What It Contains | Genealogical Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Monthly Meeting Minutes** | Births, marriages, deaths, disownments, removals | Core vital events — often the only record of a birth or death |
| **Marriage records** | Full names, dates, meeting, *signatures of all witnesses present* | Exceptionally detailed; can identify an entire community network in one document |
| **Certificates of Removal** | Issued when a member moved to a new meeting; received by the new meeting | Critical for tracking family migration between counties or states |
| **Disownment records** | Name, offense (marrying outside the faith, taking up arms, etc.) | Name the individual; often include family context |
| **Membership registers / birth registers** | Compiled lists of members and vital events | Useful overview; sometimes abstract older minutes |

Source: [Pennsylvania Church Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)

---

### What Is Digitized on FamilySearch

**Volume search (1750–1800, Religious record type)** returned one digitized volume:

| Volume | Coverage | Images | Indexed? | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (image group `001188322`) | Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, 1750–1800 | 145 images | **0% name-indexed; not full-text searchable** | Browse image-by-image only |

This volume must be browsed page by page — there is no name search. Access it at FamilySearch by searching image group `001188322`.

**FamilySearch indexed collections** overlapping 1750–1800 include:
- **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** ([collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) — useful for Quaker wills and estate inventories confirming family relationships
- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** ([collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)) — pre-1906 civil marriage records where they exist
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** ([collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)) — compiled abstracts; no images

⚠️ **Coverage gap:** Volume search and collections search returned sparse digitized material for Quaker meeting records specifically. The vast majority of Pennsylvania monthly meeting records for this era exist on **FamilySearch microfilm** (orderable through a Family History Center) or in **physical repositories** — not as searchable online collections.

---

### Primary Repositories

#### 1. Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College
- **The single largest repository of American Quaker records**
- Holds original minutes, registers, and auxiliary records for many Pennsylvania monthly meetings
- Finding aids and some digitized content: [https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library)
- Contact for access or microfilm copies

#### 2. Haverford College — Quaker & Special Collections
- Second major repository; strong in Philadelphia Yearly Meeting records and Quaker publications
- [https://www.haverford.edu/library/special-collections](https://www.haverford.edu/library/special-collections)

#### 3. Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives
- Holds records of the yearly meeting itself and some monthly meeting records
- [https://www.pym.org/historical-library/](https://www.pym.org/historical-library/)

#### 4. FamilySearch Microfilm (Family History Centers)
- FamilySearch has microfilmed a large share of Pennsylvania meeting records; these are accessible through local Family History Centers or via camera-enabled film ordering
- Start at: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)

#### 5. Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)
- Holds supplemental civil records (land, court, orphans' court) that complement meeting records

---

### Published Finding Aids — Start Here

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes**
- Abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and surrounding states into an indexed format
- Volume 2 covers Pennsylvania
- Available in print at many genealogical libraries; partially searchable online via Ancestry and other platforms
- **Use this before diving into original meeting minutes** — it may resolve a question directly or point you to the exact meeting and approximate date range to browse
- Source: [Pennsylvania Church Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)

---

### Supplemental Record Types for This Period

Because civil registration did not exist, layer these alongside meeting records:

| Record Type | Notes | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Land records / deeds** | Quakers frequently appear as buyers, sellers, and witnesses | County courthouse; PA State Archives; BLM-GLO for warrants |
| **Probate / wills** | Quaker wills often name multiple generations; executors frequently named meeting members | County orphans' court; FamilySearch collection 1999196 |
| **Tax lists** | Provincial and county tax lists survive from the 1760s–1780s; list heads of household | PA State Archives; published abstracts |
| **1790 federal census** | First federal census; lists heads of household with household counts | FamilySearch; Ancestry |
| **Court of Quarter Sessions** | Some disciplinary or property matters involving Quakers | County courthouse records |
| **Military exemption records** | Quakers were pacifists; refusal to serve in the Revolution may appear in muster or exemption records | PA State Archives; NARA |

---

### Key Research Quirks

1. **Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration until 1906.** For births, marriages, and deaths in the late 1700s, meeting records are typically the only source. Do not expect a state birth or death certificate.

2. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting oversaw meetings across multiple states** — Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and parts of Maryland. If a family lived near a state border, their meeting may be recorded across the line. Always identify which monthly meeting a family belonged to, not just the state.

3. **Certificates of removal are your migration trail.** When a Quaker family moved — even a county away — the departure meeting issued a certificate and the receiving meeting recorded its acceptance. These documents name individuals and sometimes family members, and they appear in *both* meetings' minutes.

4. **Disownment records are not a dead end.** A disowned Quaker is still documented. The offense is named (marrying a non-Quaker, joining the militia, etc.), and the individual may reappear later seeking reinstatement.

5. **Marriage witnesses = your community network.** Quaker marriage certificates were signed by everyone present. A single certificate can document dozens of neighbors, relatives, and community members — all traceable through their own meeting records.

6. **Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* is abstracted, not transcribed.** Always verify key details against the original microfilmed minutes once Hinshaw points you to the right meeting.

7. **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania** returned generic content rather than Pennsylvania-specific guidance in this session. Go directly to the specialized page: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records)

---

### Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Identify the monthly meeting** — use Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* (vol. 2) or the Friends Historical Library's online finding aids to pinpoint which meeting your family belonged to.
2. **Search Hinshaw's abstracts** for births, marriages, deaths, and removals under that meeting.
3. **Order or browse the original meeting minutes** via FamilySearch microfilm for the identified meeting and decade.
4. **Check certificates of removal** in both the sending and receiving meeting's minutes to track migration.
5. **Layer probate records** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) and tax lists to confirm family structure and approximate dates.
6. **Check the 1790 census** to establish where the family was living at the close of the period.

---

## Locality Research Guide: Pittsburgh & Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s (c. 1870–1900)
### Focus: Occupational & Industrial Records, Steel Industry Era

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 and encompasses Pittsburgh at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio Rivers. Throughout the target period (c. 1870–1900) its boundaries were stable — all county records remain under Allegheny County. Pittsburgh was incorporated as a city in 1816 and served as the county seat throughout this era.

The steel boom drew massive waves of immigrant labor — Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers — making **church records and naturalization records** just as essential as employment sources.

---

### Critical Coverage Gap: Pennsylvania Vital Registration

> ⚠️ **Pennsylvania did not require statewide birth or death registration until 1906.** For the 1870–1900 window, there are no Pennsylvania state death certificates (FamilySearch's Pennsylvania, Death Certificates collection [id: 2255317] begins in 1906 — entirely outside this target period). For births and deaths, you must rely on church registers, city directories, newspaper death notices, and census mortality schedules.

---

### 1. Federal Census Records *(Indexed — High Priority)*

The federal censuses of **1870, 1880, and 1900** all recorded each person's occupation, making them the backbone of any occupational search for steel-era Pittsburgh. Each lists place of birth and parentage.

- **1870 and 1880**: Available on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch; 1880 has full Soundex index.
- **1890**: Almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921. This gap must be bridged using 1880/1900 censuses, city directories, and church records together.
- **1900**: Full Soundex index available; includes month/year of birth, years in the United States, and naturalization status — particularly valuable for immigrant steelworkers.
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885)**: Record deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration and can substitute for absent death certificates.

**Access:** Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/); FamilySearch; National Archives at Philadelphia (for original images).

---

### 2. Industrial & Occupational Records *(Largely Physical — Key Repositories Required)*

This is the most distinctive record class for this research and the most fragmented online.

| Source | What It Contains | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Hiring dates, wages, job titles, sometimes age/nativity | Fragmentary — some survive at the **Heinz History Center** and **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives** |
| **Union membership lists** | Names, occupations, local lodge, sometimes address | Heinz History Center; Rivers of Steel; union national archives |
| **City directories** | Name, occupation, employer, home address — annual snapshots | Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh has directories from the 1810s; also on Ancestry.com |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Lists of workers by plant, sometimes with accident records | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg |

> ⚠️ **Company employment records are largely undigitized and fragmentary.** Online searches will not surface them. A physical visit to (or inquiry with) the **Heinz History Center** (1212 Smallman Street, Pittsburgh) or the **Rivers of Steel Heritage Area** is typically required. Not all firms' records survived.

**FamilySearch Wiki reference:** [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)

---

### 3. City Directories *(Browse-Only / Partially Indexed)*

Pittsburgh city directories were published annually and are one of the most reliable intercensal tools — especially important given the destroyed 1890 census. They list occupation and employer for every adult male head of household, and increasingly for women in later decades.

- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds an unbroken run from the 1810s through the 20th century.
- Many volumes are also available on **Ancestry.com** and partially on Google Books.
- Use year-by-year to track job changes, migration within the county, and co-residence patterns.

---

### 4. Marriage Records *(Indexed — Good Coverage)*

Three FamilySearch collections cover marriages overlapping this period:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range | Records |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | 1921317 | 1885–1950 | 524,189 |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | 1571957 | 1677–1950 | 312,045 |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | 1502909 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 (no images) |

Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317 and https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957

---

### 5. Probate Records *(Indexed — Good Coverage)*

**Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (FamilySearch id: 1999196) covers wills, inventories, and estate administration — 893,214 records with images. Useful for identifying property, naming adult children, and locating extended family networks.

Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196

---

### 6. Church Records *(Critical for Immigrant Steelworker Families)*

For the immigrant communities that staffed Pittsburgh's mills, **ethnic Catholic parish registers are often the richest family source** — recording baptisms, marriages, and burials with detail that compensates for absent civil registration.

Key communities and their parishes:
- **Polish**: St. Stanislaus Kostka, Polish Hill
- **Slovak and Croatian**: Multiple parishes in mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport)
- **Italian**: St. Anthony of Padua and others
- **Irish and German**: Earlier-established parishes throughout the county

> ⚠️ Many ethnic parish registers were kept in the **native language** (Polish, Slovak, Latin). Access varies: some are microfilmed by FamilySearch, others remain in parish or diocesan custody. Contact the **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** for holdings. FamilySearch microfilm holdings for Pennsylvania church records exist but coverage at the individual-parish level is uneven.

---

### 7. Naturalization Records *(Physical + Some Indexed)*

The massive immigrant workforce means naturalization records are a high-value source. Pre-1906, a worker could naturalize in **any court of record** — county, state, or federal — so searches must cover all three.

- **Allegheny County Courthouse**: County court naturalizations
- **National Archives at Philadelphia** (701 Market Street): Federal court naturalizations and passenger arrival lists
- FamilySearch holds some indexed Pennsylvania naturalization series; search by county

**FamilySearch Wiki reference:** [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)

---

### 8. Newspapers *(Browse-Only / Partially Indexed)*

Pittsburgh had active daily newspapers throughout the period (*Pittsburgh Post*, *Pittsburgh Dispatch*, *Pittsburgh Press*). Useful for:
- Death notices and obituaries (substitute for absent death certificates)
- Strike and labor unrest coverage (may name individual workers)
- Accident reports from mills (may name injured or killed workers)

**Access:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); some holdings also at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh and on Chronicling America (Library of Congress).

---

### 9. Military Records *(Indexed)*

For veterans of the Civil War (1861–1865) who appear in your 1870–1900 window:
- **Service records and pension files**: National Archives (search via Fold3: https://www.fold3.com/)
- **Veterans' schedules** of the 1880 census enumerate surviving soldiers and sailors

---

### 10. Land & Tax Records *(Physical — County Courthouse)*

Deed books and annual tax assessment lists are held at the **Allegheny County Courthouse** (414 Grant Street, Pittsburgh). Tax records can locate a family in a specific ward year by year and sometimes note occupation.

---

### Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** | Company/industrial records, immigration records, city directories | In-person; some finding aids online at heinzhistorycenter.org |
| **Rivers of Steel Heritage Area** | Steel-industry company records, union records | In-person/inquiry |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1810s–), local history, newspapers | In-person; some digital |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Deeds, naturalizations, court records | In-person |
| **National Archives — Philadelphia** | Federal court naturalizations, passenger lists, census originals | In-person; many indexed on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** | Factory inspector reports, state-level records | In-person; some digital via Pennsylvania State Archives portal |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Catholic parish registers | By inquiry |
| **FamilySearch** | Marriage records, probate, some church records | Online — familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, city directories, passenger lists | Subscription |

---

### Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No statewide birth or death registration before 1906.** Church records and city directories are the primary substitutes for civil vital registration throughout the entire 1870–1900 period.
2. **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed.** Plan around this gap using 1880 and 1900 censuses plus annual city directories and church baptism/burial records.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations may appear in county, state, or federal court** — search all three jurisdictions before concluding a worker did not naturalize.
4. **Industrial/company employment records are fragmentary and mostly undigitized.** Online searches will not surface them; contact the Heinz History Center or Rivers of Steel directly.
5. **Ethnic parish records are often in the native language** (Polish, Slovak, Latin). Budget for translation or recruit a language specialist.
6. **Mill-town families may have lived outside Pittsburgh city limits** — Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, and Duquesne were separate municipalities with their own churches and cemeteries. Confirm the specific mill town before narrowing the search.

---

### Digitization Coverage Note

The FamilySearch tools returned no place_population data for Allegheny County and the wiki_place_page tool served only generic content for this survey. The specific industrial and immigration record guidance above comes from the [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy) FamilySearch Wiki page (retrieved via wiki_search). The most distinctive record classes for this research — company employment records, union lists, and factory inspector reports — have no significant online presence and require physical repository visits. FamilySearch's Pennsylvania-level digital holdings are strongest for marriage and probate records; vital registration coverage for the 1870–1900 period is a real gap.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic (c. 1785–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682, one of Pennsylvania's three original counties. Both the city and county date from that year (`place_search` dateRange: +1682/).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (state from 1787; colony before)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 in the city proper at the time of the epidemic. The outbreak killed approximately 5,000 people — roughly one-tenth of the population — between August and November 1793. ([Wikipedia: Yellow fever epidemic of 1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793))
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic commercial port; merchants, artisans, shipping, trade, printing and publishing. Philadelphia was the national capital 1790–1800.
- **Ethnic composition:** English, Welsh, German, Scots-Irish, Irish, Swedish (centered on Gloria Dei congregation), free and enslaved Black Philadelphians.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Society of Friends (Quakers), Presbyterian, Catholic, Methodist, Baptist, German Reformed, Lutheran, Jewish.
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November); Philadelphia served as the U.S. national capital during the entire epidemic period. Thousands fled the city; those who remained were documented in death registers, church burial records, and the minutes of the citizens' Committee. Mayor Matthew Clarkson and physician Benjamin Rush left detailed accounts of the crisis. ([Wikipedia: Yellow fever epidemic of 1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793))

---

## Boundary changes

- **No boundary changes** to Philadelphia County occurred during the target period (1785–1810); the county has existed since 1682.
- In 1793, the **city of Philadelphia** was a distinct municipality embedded within the county. Surrounding townships — Northern Liberties, Southwark, and others — were part of the county but outside the city corporation. Records created in these surrounding townships may be held at the county level, not the city level. Search both city and county repositories for families near the urban fringe.
- The city and county were consolidated into a single jurisdiction by the 1854 Consolidation Act — this does not affect records created in 1793, but modern finding aids may list pre-1854 records under either the city or the county name.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date — statewide:** Pennsylvania did not have **statewide** civil registration until **1906**. This is confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki: church records are "the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906." ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records exist for the epidemic year at any governmental level. Church records are the primary and nearly exclusive source of vital events.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers (see below); Mathew Carey's published list of the dead; the citizens' Committee minutes; Bush Hill hospital records.
- **Post-period note:** Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968 (FamilySearch collection 2255317) begins after this period entirely; useful for locating descendants but not epidemic victims themselves.

### Church records ⭐ *Primary source for 1793*

The FamilySearch Wiki identifies church records as the central genealogical source for this period and specifically names several congregations in the context of the epidemic:

- **Congregations with confirmed epidemic-era burial relevance:** Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal, founded 1695) and Gloria Dei/Old Swedes' (Swedish Lutheran, founded 1677). Other Philadelphia congregations also maintained burial registers. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials/interments
- **Indexes:** The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records; many colonial and early national registers have been transcribed and published. ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Where held:** Individual parish archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania; some transcribed volumes at the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania and via Ancestry.com partner collections.
- **Language:** Primarily English; Gloria Dei early registers in Swedish and German; German-language congregations kept records in German.
- **FamilySearch digitization status:** The `collections_search` for Pennsylvania (1750–1820) did not return a named, usable Philadelphia church-record collection — this is a gap. Church records for this period on FamilySearch may be browse-only images within broader Pennsylvania or regional microfilm holdings. Check the FamilySearch Catalog under "Philadelphia County — Church Records" for individual congregation films.

### Epidemic-specific records ⭐ *Unique to the 1793 outbreak*

These are the most targeted sources for tracing families affected by the epidemic, confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)) and Wikipedia:

| Record | Description | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever"** (1793) | Published pamphlet with lists of the dead; multiple editions | Historical Society of Pennsylvania; digitized editions online |
| **Minutes and reports of the citizens' Committee** | Documented relief efforts, names of those who stayed, fled, or died | Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania |
| **Bush Hill hospital records** | Records of the epidemic's primary hospital | Philadelphia City Archives; Historical Society of Pennsylvania |
| **Mayor Clarkson's accounts and correspondence** | Detailed civic documentation of the crisis | Philadelphia City Archives |
| **Dr. Benjamin Rush's papers** | Rush documented the epidemic extensively | Historical Society of Pennsylvania |

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The **1790** census (first national census) and the **1800** census bracket the epidemic — critical for establishing household composition immediately before and after. These did not appear in `collections_search` for Pennsylvania (they are indexed nationally, not at the state level). Search via FamilySearch's federal census collections or Ancestry.com directly.
- **Mortality schedules:** Federal mortality schedules did not begin until 1850 — no mortality schedule exists for 1793.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct state censuses during this period.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** Pennsylvania tax assessments for Philadelphia County survive for the colonial and early national period and can substitute for missing intercensal years. Sudden disappearance from tax rolls in 1793–1794 may indicate epidemic death or flight. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Probate and court records

- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection id: [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) — 893,214 records with 446,607 images, available free at FamilySearch. This collection spans the target period and should be searched for Philadelphia County filings in 1793–1795.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed (893K records) with substantial imaging (446K images); full name-indexing coverage for the 1793 window cannot be confirmed without `volume_search` data — browse the images if a name search returns no results.
- **Epidemic value:** The epidemic generated a surge of estate filings in late 1793 and 1794. Probate records often name heirs, relationships, and creditors — a rich source for reconstructing families disrupted by epidemic death.
- **Held at:** Philadelphia Orphans' Court (county level); Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Marriage records

- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (id: [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)) — 312,045 records, 156,023 images; free at FamilySearch. Overlaps the target period.
- **FamilySearch collection confirmed:** **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (id: [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)) — 198,765 records, **no images** (index only); free at FamilySearch. Useful for finding a marriage entry but you will need to locate the original elsewhere.
- **Note:** Civil marriage registration in Pennsylvania before 1906 was at the county level through the Court of Common Pleas. Church marriages are the primary source for most of this period and may not appear in civil collections.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; grants originated with the Penn proprietors, then the Commonwealth).
- **Types:** Deeds, warrants, patents, mortgages held at the county Recorder of Deeds (Philadelphia County) and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Date range:** From 1682.
- **Epidemic value:** Land transfers in 1793–1795 may document deaths indirectly — heirs conveying inherited property, sudden sales by families fleeing the city, or estate settlements. Deed grantors who die mid-transaction appear in both deed and probate records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (ended 1783 — veterans are present in Philadelphia in 1793); Quasi-War with France (1798–1800).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA. Pension files often contain family and biographical detail useful for tracing Revolutionary War veterans who survived the epidemic.
- **Access:** Fold3 (subscription) — confirmed in `external_links_search`; NARA (archives.gov) — confirmed in `external_links_search`.

### Cemetery records

- **Context:** The epidemic created unusual burial circumstances — many victims were interred quickly in existing church burial grounds and in areas outside the normal city limits.
- **Church burial registers are more reliable than grave markers** for 1793 victims; many epidemic burials lack individual monuments.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) — confirmed in `external_links_search`; useful for later-period graves and for locating descendants.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers for Christ Church, Gloria Dei, St. Peter's, and other congregations; originals at individual church archives and at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

### Newspaper records

- **Context:** Philadelphia was a major publishing center; multiple newspapers covered the epidemic and published weekly lists of the dead.
- **Online access:** Newspapers.com (subscription) — confirmed in `external_links_search`; also Chronicling America at the Library of Congress (free).
- **Content value:** Death notices, obituaries, notices of property sales, departure announcements (many families published notices of their departure from the city), public health committee announcements. Newspapers for August–November 1793 are among the most direct sources for names of those who died or fled.

### Immigration and naturalization records

- **Context:** Philadelphia was a major port of entry. Historians have linked the epidemic's origin to arrivals from Saint-Domingue (present-day Haiti); passenger records from 1793 may identify families who arrived just before or during the outbreak.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at NARA; pre-1906 naturalization petitions filed in any Philadelphia court of record.
- **Access:** NARA (archives.gov) — confirmed in `external_links_search`; some lists digitized on Ancestry.com.

### Organizational and poor-relief records

- **Committee for Relief of the Sick and Distressed:** The citizens' Committee documented aid recipients and distributed funds; minutes and reports held at the Philadelphia City Archives and HSP — confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)).
- **Overseers of the Poor:** Philadelphia's poor-relief records document those who received public assistance during the epidemic; held at the Philadelphia City Archives.
- **Free African Society records:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) played a documented major role in epidemic relief; their records at HSP may document Black Philadelphians otherwise difficult to trace in this period.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (893K records / 446K images); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (312K records / 156K images); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (198K records / index only) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census 1790 and 1800; passenger lists; GSP church record indexes | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service and pension records (Revolutionary War veterans in Philadelphia) | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Federal records: passenger lists, military service | Free finding aids; fees for copies |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Committee minutes, Bush Hill hospital records, city government records, Overseers of the Poor records, tax assessments | In-person; some records available via written request |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Manuscript epidemic sources, church records, Benjamin Rush papers, Free African Society records, Mathew Carey papers | In-person research; some online via HSP Digital Library |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)** | State government records, tax lists, land records, court records | In-person; some online |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** | Compiled indexes to Philadelphia church records; published transcription volumes | In-person; partner collections via Ancestry.com |
| **Individual church archives** | Christ Church, Gloria Dei (Old Swedes'), St. Peter's, and others — original baptism, marriage, burial registers | Contact each church; consult published GSP transcriptions first |

---

## Records NOT online

The following are confirmed by tool results to exist but are not fully available in any online database:

- **Bush Hill hospital records** — physical at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP
- **Citizens' Committee minutes in full** — manuscript at Philadelphia City Archives and HSP; not fully digitized
- **Overseers of the Poor records** — Philadelphia City Archives
- **Philadelphia County tax assessments (1793 period)** — Philadelphia City Archives and Pennsylvania State Archives; digitization coverage not confirmed by available tools
- **Many individual church burial registers** — while some have been published or transcribed by GSP, originals and records of smaller congregations remain physical-only

---

## Known record losses

- No major courthouse fire or systematic loss for Philadelphia County's core records in this period was returned by tool results; Philadelphia County's records are generally considered well-preserved.
- The epidemic itself disrupted normal record-keeping. Gaps or irregular entries in church registers for August–November 1793 are expected — clergy and sextons were also among those who fled or died.
- `wiki_place_page` for Pennsylvania returned only generic content across all four sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips); no Pennsylvania-specific digitization loss data was returned.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the epidemic's published sources.** Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793) and the Committee minutes are the most direct tools for identifying victims by name — confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)).

2. **Church records before 1906 are your primary vital source.** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration until 1906. For 1793, burial registers from Christ Church, Gloria Dei, and other Philadelphia congregations are the main record of deaths. Check GSP's published indexes before searching original registers ([Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)).

3. **Search probate records for a 1793–1795 filing surge.** The epidemic generated a spike in estate filings. Search the Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 collection on FamilySearch (collection [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196)) for Philadelphia County entries filed in that window. Probate files often name spouses, children, creditors, and witnesses.

4. **Bracket the epidemic with the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.** Comparing household composition before and after the epidemic can reveal who was lost — members present in 1790 absent in 1800, or changes in household head. Both censuses are indexed and searchable on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.

5. **Philadelphia newspapers carried weekly death lists during the epidemic.** Papers such as Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser and the Federal Gazette published names of the dead and notices of families fleeing. Search Newspapers.com and Chronicling America for August–November 1793 Philadelphia papers.

6. **Families who fled may have left records in surrounding counties.** Many Philadelphians evacuated to Germantown, Chester County, Montgomery County, and other neighboring areas. Their departure and return may be documented in adjacent county repositories and in the Philadelphia newspapers.

7. **For Black Philadelphians, start with the Free African Society records.** The society organized relief during the epidemic; their records at HSP document members of Philadelphia's African American community.

8. **Check both city and county repositories.** In 1793, the city of Philadelphia and the county were separate jurisdictions. Families in Northern Liberties, Southwark, or other surrounding townships generated county-level records, not city-level ones.

# Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Locality Research Guide
### Families Affected by the Great Chicago Fire of 1871

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Chicago sits in **Cook County, Illinois** (standardPlace: `Chicago, Cook, Illinois, United States`). The county was organized in 1831; Chicago was incorporated as a city in 1837.

**The core research problem:** On October 8–10, 1871, the Great Chicago Fire burned 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, and left more than 100,000 residents homeless. It destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, taking with it most of the city's pre-fire official records — deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Many church registers were also lost. This creates a hard wall for direct records before October 1871; the research strategy for fire-affected families centers on **records held outside Chicago** and **post-fire substitutes and reconstructions**.

---

## Critical Quirks — Read Before Searching

> ⚠️ **Most pre-1871 Cook County vital records are gone.** Do not expect to find pre-fire birth or death certificates. The fire destroyed the courthouse where they were held.
>
> ⚠️ **Illinois statewide vital registration did not begin until 1916.** Cook County began its own local registration from 1871 — but the very earliest post-fire records (late 1871) may be sparse or incomplete. Source: [Illinois Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Statewide_Registration)
>
> ⚠️ **The 1890 federal census was also largely destroyed** (in a 1921 Commerce Department fire), eliminating a second recovery anchor. The 1870 census is your best pre-fire population snapshot.
>
> ⚠️ **The Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-file deeds. These reconstructed filings, not originals, are what survive for pre-fire property ownership.

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. Federal Census Records
**The single most important pre-fire source.** Federal census originals were held in Washington, D.C. — they survived the fire intact.

| Census Year | Coverage | Notes |
|-------------|----------|-------|
| 1850 | ✅ Survived | Names all household members |
| 1860 | ✅ Survived | Names all household members |
| 1870 | ✅ Survived | Best pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families |
| 1880 | ✅ Survived | First post-fire full enumeration |
| 1890 | ❌ Destroyed | Lost in 1921 NARA fire; fragments only |
| 1900 | ✅ Available | Full recovery; very useful for post-fire families |

- **Access:** FamilySearch (free), Ancestry.com (subscription)
- **Digitization:** Indexed + images for all surviving years
- **Source:** [U.S. Federal Census Collection — Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)

---

### 2. Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**Pre-1871:** Essentially none survive at the county level. Destroyed in the fire.

**Post-1871 (Cook County local registration):**
FamilySearch holds three indexed collections covering the recovery period and beyond:
- **Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** — ~1,450,000 records (collection ID: 2024189)
- **Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947** — ~980,000 records (collection ID: 1913456)
- **Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920** — ~620,000 records (collection ID: 1756321)

- **Digitization:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch
- **Physical repository:** Cook County Clerk's Office, Chicago
- **Note:** The earliest post-fire records (late 1871) may have gaps as the registration system was re-established. If you don't find someone there, move immediately to church records.

---

### 3. Church Records — Primary Substitute for Pre-Fire Vital Events

For pre-1871 baptisms, marriages, and burials, church registers are the principal surviving source. Some parishes lay outside the burn zone; others were re-established and reconstructed their registers from memory or duplicate copies.

FamilySearch holds:
- **Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925** — ~285,000 records (collection ID: 1803978); indexed + images

Key denominational repositories:
- **Catholic:** Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives and Records Center, Archdiocese of Chicago — holds parish registers for Catholic congregations. Many pre-fire Catholic registers partially survive.
- **Lutheran, Episcopal, and other Protestant denominations:** Check the denomination's own regional archive and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

Source: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)

---

### 4. Property / Deed Records — Burnt Record Act Reconstructions

The **Burnt Record Act (1872)** required all Chicago-area property owners to re-register their deeds. These reconstructed filings are the primary evidence of pre-fire property ownership and often name family members and sellers in chains of title.

FamilySearch has a **partially indexed** volume of post-fire property re-recordings:
- Image group **009982111** — 112 images, **41% name-indexed**, not full-text searchable — covers 1871–1880, Post-fire Property Re-recordings for Chicago, Cook, Illinois.

A second volume covers pre-fire reconstructed court records:
- Image group **009982110** — 38 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable, browse-only** — covers 1865–1871, Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies). Must be browsed image by image; there is no name search.

- **Physical repository:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University
- **Also useful:** Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records (pre-fire property ownership), held at the **Chicago History Museum**

---

### 5. City Directories — A Key Pre-Fire Substitute

Chicago city directories were published from **1839 onward** and survived the fire. They list heads of household (and often other adult residents), occupation, and address — providing a year-by-year population snapshot. They can anchor a family's presence in Chicago before the fire when no official records survive.

- **Repository:** Newberry Library, Chicago (primary collection)
- **Online:** Some years digitized on Ancestry.com and the Internet Archive
- **Digitization:** Varies by year; many are browse-only scans

---

### 6. Naturalization Records

Cook County **Circuit Court and Superior Court** naturalization records survive from the **1840s** — they were not all held in the courthouse building destroyed by the fire, or copies survived elsewhere.

- **Repository:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University; also microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Also:** NARA holds federal court naturalization records; after September 27, 1906, all naturalizations went through federal courts
- **Pre-1906 caveat:** Naturalization could occur in any court — federal, state, county, or municipal — so check all levels

Source: [Illinois Vital Records — Substitute Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Illinois_Vital_Records#Substitute_Records)

---

### 7. Military Records

Not affected by the fire — federal military records were held in Washington. Essential for identifying men who served in the Civil War (1861–1865), which overlaps with the pre-fire Chicago generation.

- **Service records and pension files:** National Archives (NARA), Washington, D.C.; digitized on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/)
- **Illinois state military records:** Illinois State Archives, Springfield
- **Draft registrations (Civil War):** NARA; available on FamilySearch and Ancestry

---

### 8. Probate Records

Cook County probate files (wills, inventories, administration records) were largely destroyed in the 1871 fire. Post-fire probate records survive from 1871 onward.

- **Repository:** Cook County Circuit Court Clerk (Probate Division); IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University holds older microfilmed records
- **Pre-fire gap:** If probate evidence is needed for a pre-1871 ancestor, use federal census estate values and city directory occupation listings as substitute indicators

---

### 9. Newspapers

Contemporary newspaper coverage of the fire is extensive — including lists of fire victims, "lost relatives" notices, and refugee reports. Post-fire papers also published reunion notices and insurance claim news.

- **Repository:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription); Newberry Library (Chicago Tribune, Chicago Times, and others on microfilm); ProQuest Historical Newspapers
- **Chicago Tribune** archives from 1849 onward are particularly useful
- **Digitization:** Partially indexed + full-text searchable on Newspapers.com; microfilm browse-only at Newberry

---

### 10. Cemetery Records

Cemetery offices maintained their own registers, largely independent of the courthouse. Pre-fire burials in Chicago's major cemeteries (Rosehill, Graceland, Oak Woods, and others) are often documented.

- **Online:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) — indexed transcriptions with photos; useful for dates and family connections
- **Physical:** Individual cemetery offices; Cook County death records (post-1871) often note cemetery
- **Note:** The city relocated Calvary Cemetery and other early burial grounds in the 1850s-60s; some records of those transfers survive

---

### 11. Immigration and Passenger Records

Chicago in 1871 had a large immigrant population (German, Irish, Scandinavian, Bohemian). Passenger arrival records were kept at the port of entry, not Chicago — and therefore survived the fire entirely.

- **Repository:** NARA; passenger lists digitized on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch
- **Port of entry:** Most arrivals to Chicago came through New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island) or New Orleans, then inland by rail or river
- **FamilySearch:** Free indexed access to many passenger lists

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records, fire photographs, personal papers, manuscripts | In-person; some digitized |
| **Newberry Library, Chicago** | City directories (1839+), maps, local histories, newspapers on microfilm | In-person; some digitized |
| **IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County records post-1871 (probate, naturalization, court) | In-person; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers | In-person by appointment |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 | In-person + online |
| **Illinois State Archives, Springfield** | Military, state census fragments, land patents | In-person; some online |
| **FamilySearch** | Cook County church records, birth/death/marriage 1871+, census, microfilm | Free online |
| **NARA** | Federal census, military, naturalization, passenger lists | In-person + digitized partners |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, city directories, newspapers, military records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records, grave photos | Free online |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers including Chicago Tribune | Subscription |

---
