## Louisiana Locality Guide: French Colonial Period (1700s)

### Jurisdictional Context

The 1700s in Louisiana spans **two colonial regimes**, which directly affects what records exist, what language they're in, and where they're held:

| Period | Authority | Language |
|---|---|---|
| 1699–1762 | **French** (Colony of New France) | French |
| 1762–1800 | **Spanish** (Treaty of Fontainebleau) | Spanish |
| 1800–1803 | Brief French return; Louisiana Purchase 1803 | French / English |

France claimed the Mississippi basin in 1682; New Orleans was founded in 1718. Colonial administration ran through the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)**, which handled civil, legal, and land matters. There were no counties — the territory was organized into **districts and military posts**, not the civil-parish system Louisiana uses today. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church under both regimes.

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** If your ancestor lived in Louisiana in the second half of the 1700s (post-1762), their records will be in **Spanish**, not French, and may be filed in a different administrative series. Search both the French-era and Spanish-era record sets — they are related but distinct.

---

### Record Types, Repositories & Access

#### 1. Catholic Parish Registers — **PRIMARY SOURCE**
**Baptisms, marriages, and burials**

The Catholic Church was the sole keeper of vital records during the entire French (and Spanish) colonial period. No civil registration existed.

- **Registers begin:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) has registers from **1720**.
- **Code Noir requirement:** The Black Code required baptism of all enslaved persons, making Catholic registers a critical source for African-descended families in this period as well.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — ~987,654 records, ~493,827 images. This collection's earliest records (1718–1762) fall squarely in the French colonial period.
- **Access level:** Indexed with images on FamilySearch — searchable by name.
- **Language warning:** Records are in **Latin and French** (French period) or **Latin and Spanish** (post-1762). A researcher must be able to read these languages or use transcribed editions.
- **Other repositories:** Individual parish archives and the **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** also hold originals or copies.

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Not all colonial-era parishes are represented in the FamilySearch collection. Rural posts and mission stations may have separate or incomplete registers — or none at all for remote areas.

---

#### 2. Superior Council Records (Conseil Supérieur)
**Land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories**

The Superior Council was the colony's governing body — functionally a combined civil court, legislature, and land office. Its records include:
- Land concessions (grants) to settlers
- Civil court proceedings and disputes
- Marriage contracts and estate inventories (analogous to probate)
- Criminal proceedings

- **Held at:** **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, Louisiana. Partially digitized.
- **Access level:** Partially digitized; physical visit or correspondence with the Louisiana Historical Center required for full access.
- **Language:** French (pre-1762); Spanish (post-1762, under the Spanish Cabildo).
- **Source:** FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records (1699–1762)" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** After 1762, the Spanish replaced the Superior Council with the **Cabildo**. Spanish-era governance records are a separate administrative series, also held at the Louisiana Historical Center.

---

#### 3. New Orleans Notarial Archives
**Contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions**

The New Orleans Notarial Archives is the **oldest continuous notarial office in North America**, with records from the **1730s** onward. Notarial acts in French (and later Spanish) civil law covered a wide range of life events that in common-law states would leave no record at all: marriage contracts, business agreements, property sales, manumissions, and wills.

- **Held at:** **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**, New Orleans, Louisiana. Public access provided.
- **Access level:** Physical repository; not fully digitized online. Researchers should contact the archives directly for remote access options.
- **Language:** French (pre-1762); Spanish (post-1762).
- **Source:** FamilySearch Wiki, "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))

---

#### 4. Land Records
**French concessions and Spanish land grants**

Colonial land grants followed French civil law traditions — not English common law. The primary compiled sources are:

- **American State Papers: Public Lands** — Documents French concessions and Spanish land grants; published and widely available in research libraries and on archive.org.
- **Louisiana State Land Office** — Holds additional land grant documentation.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — ~456,789 records, ~228,394 images. The date range starts 1756, capturing the final French colonial years and the full Spanish period. Includes estate-related land documents alongside probate materials.

---

#### 5. Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) — France
**Administrative correspondence, colonial census rolls, emigration records**

For the French colonial period specifically, the **French national overseas archives in Aix-en-Provence** hold records that exist nowhere else:

- Administrative correspondence between the colony and France
- **Dénombrements** (colonial census rolls) listing heads of household, family members, enslaved persons, and livestock
- Emigration and passenger records for colonists arriving from France
- Military rosters for colonial troops

- **Held at:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Some materials available through their online portal at [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr).
- **Access level:** Physical repository with a partial online portal. Remote ordering of digital copies is possible for some series.
- **Language:** French throughout.

> This repository is **essential** for tracing immigrant origins — if your ancestor came from France, Acadia, or the Caribbean colonies, ANOM may document their departure point and family background.

---

#### 6. FamilySearch Collections Overlapping the Target Period

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) | 1718–1925 | ~987,654 | ~493,827 | Indexed + images |
| [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) | 1756–1984 | ~456,789 | ~228,394 | Indexed + images |

**Post-colonial collections (not applicable for 1700s research, background context only):**
- Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 — begins after Louisiana Purchase
- Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 — begins after Louisiana Purchase

---

#### 7. Supplementary Record Types

| Record Type | Where to Look | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Military rosters** | ANOM (France); Louisiana Historical Center | Colonial militia and regular troop lists |
| **Slave records / manumissions** | Superior Council records; Notarial Archives; Catholic registers | Code Noir baptism requirement makes church records key |
| **Published genealogies & compiled records** | Genealogical Society of New Orleans; Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society | Much colonial-era material has been transcribed and published |
| **Maps and districts** | Louisiana State Archives; Library of Congress | Essential for identifying which post or district your ancestor lived in |

---

### Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | Location | What It Holds |
|---|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** | Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans, LA | Superior Council records; Spanish Cabildo records |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives** | New Orleans, LA | Notarial acts from 1730s onward |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | New Orleans, LA | Catholic parish registers |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Online | Church Records 1718+; Probate Records 1756+ |
| **ANOM** | Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative records, census rolls |
| **Louisiana State Archives** | Baton Rouge, LA | Later colonial and territorial materials |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Washington, DC / online | Post-1803 federal records; American State Papers |

---

### Researcher's Checklist for French Colonial Louisiana

1. **Identify the district or post** where your ancestor lived — the colony was not organized by parish during the French period. Maps of colonial Louisiana posts will help.
2. **Search Catholic registers first** — they are the only vital records for this period. Begin with FamilySearch's Church Records 1718–1925 collection.
3. **Check notarial and Superior Council records** for property, contracts, and estates — these fill in life events that church registers don't capture.
4. **Know the language:** French before 1762, Spanish after. If you can't read these, look for transcribed or translated editions published by Louisiana genealogical societies.
5. **If the family immigrated from France**, go to ANOM for origin documentation and emigration records.
6. **Don't ignore the Spanish period (1762–1800):** if the family was in Louisiana for the whole century, half their records are in Spanish under an entirely different administrative structure.

# Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide

**Core counties:** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland (anthracite); Fayette, Westmoreland, Washington, Allegheny (bituminous)

## Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania's coal region spans two distinct fields:

- **Anthracite (northeastern PA):** Schuylkill County (formed 1811), Carbon County (formed 1843), Luzerne County, and Northumberland County. **Lackawanna County was split from Luzerne County in 1878.** Records for the Scranton and Carbondale area before 1878 are filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne first for any event before that year.
- **Bituminous (western PA):** Fayette, Westmoreland, Washington, and Allegheny counties; these generated a similar but separate body of records.

The region drew massive immigrant waves: Irish, Welsh, and German miners from the 1840s–1870s, followed by Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Italians, and Ukrainians in the 1880s–1900s. The ethnic composition of a mining town directly determines which church records survive and where they are held.

## ⚠️ Critical Quirk: No Statewide Birth/Death Registration Until 1906

Pennsylvania **did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1906** — well after the late-1800s target window ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)). For deaths and births in the 1870–1905 period, **church records are the primary source**, not government vital records. Two county exceptions: Philadelphia began local registration in 1860; Allegheny County (Pittsburgh) in 1870. No equivalent county-level vital registration is documented for the anthracite coal counties in the FamilySearch wiki results.

| Record | Counties | Coverage | Access Level | Where Held |
|--------|----------|----------|--------------|------------|
| Mine Worker Employment Cards | Schuylkill | 1870–1900 | **Indexed + Full-Text** (95% searchable; image group 002240015, 410 images) | FamilySearch |
| Mine Accident Reports | Luzerne | 1870–1895 | **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text; image group 002240016, 287 images) | FamilySearch |
| Colliery Payroll Ledgers | Lackawanna | 1878–1900 | **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text; image group 002240017, 199 images) | FamilySearch |
| Annual Mine Inspector Reports | Statewide | 1870–1900s | Physical + partial microfilm | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg |
| Company payrolls, accident reports | Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna | Fragmentary | Physical | PA State Archives; Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton |
| UMWA membership rolls & grievance files | Statewide | 1890+ | Physical/archival | UMWA archives; some at PA State Archives |

**Note on volume search:** The volume search returned 23 total digitized volumes for this region (1860–1910 window) but only the first page of results. Additional volumes likely exist — browse the full set at FamilySearch for each county.

The **Annual Mine Inspector Reports** (published from 1870) are especially valuable: they list fatal accident victims by name, age, nationality, and cause of death ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).

---

### 2. Church Records *(the most important vital source for 1870–1905)*

Pennsylvania's mining towns were organized around ethnic parishes. The church register — not the courthouse — is where you will find baptisms, marriages, and burials for the late 1800s.

| Ethnic community | Typical denomination | Notes |
|-----------------|----------------------|-------|
| Irish | Roman Catholic | Dioceses of Scranton (1868) and Allentown cover most of the anthracite region |
| Welsh | Welsh Congregational / Presbyterian | Registers often in Welsh |
| German | Lutheran / Reformed / Catholic | Often bilingual records |
| Polish | Roman Catholic (Polish national parishes) | Registers often in Polish or Latin |
| Lithuanian | Roman Catholic | Registers often in Lithuanian or Latin |
| Slovak/Ukrainian | Greek Catholic / Roman Catholic | Some registers in Cyrillic or Latin |
| Italian | Roman Catholic | Later arrivals, 1890s+ |

**Repositories:** FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church registers. Contact the Diocese of Scranton Archives (for Lackawanna/Luzerne Catholic records) and the Diocese of Allentown (for Schuylkill/Carbon Catholic records) for undigitized material. The [Historical Society of Schuylkill County](https://www.hss.org) and the [Anthracite Heritage Museum, Scranton](https://anthracitemuseum.org) hold local church collections.

**Access:** Church records are not systematically indexed at FamilySearch for these counties in this period. Expect browse-only or physical-access-only for many registers. Verify which volumes exist before traveling.

---

### 3. Marriage Records *(county-level, colonial period onward)*

Marriage licenses and bonds were kept at the **county courthouse** from the colonial period. FamilySearch has indexed collections covering this period:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | FamilySearch Link |
|-----------|-----------|---------|--------|-------------------|
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | [Collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) |
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | 312,045 | [Collection 1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | None (index only) | [Collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) |

For marriages in the 1870–1885 window, prioritize the Civil Marriages and Compiled Marriages collections. Original county marriage records are also held at county courthouses and at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### 4. Death Records *(post-period, but close)*

The statewide **Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968** collection (FamilySearch [Collection 2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317), 4,218,763 records and images) is the first systematic death record for Pennsylvania — but it begins in **1906**, just after the target window. For deaths 1870–1905, the sources are:
- Church burial registers (see above)
- Federal census **mortality schedules** (1870 and 1880 schedules list individuals who died in the prior year — available on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch)
- Cemetery records (see below)
- Mine accident reports and Mine Inspector reports (for workplace deaths)

---

### 5. Federal Census Records

The decennial censuses of **1870, 1880, 1890, 1900** are your backbone sources. The 1880 census is fully indexed and free at FamilySearch. Note:
- **1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed** — only fragments survive. Pennsylvania had no state census to fill this gap.
- The 1880 census lists **occupation** and can identify miners; the 1900 census adds immigration year and years of U.S. residence.
- **1880 Soundex** covers households with children under 10 only — do not rely on it alone; browse the full schedule for the mining town.
- Census records are available on Ancestry.com ([U.S. Federal Census — Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) and FamilySearch.

---

### 6. Naturalization Records *(critical for immigrant miners)*

Most late-19th-century miners naturalized through **county courts of common pleas** near the mines. Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are documented at the Pennsylvania State Archives ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)). Before 1906, naturalization could occur in any court of record — check federal, state, and local courts.

After **September 27, 1906**, all naturalizations moved to federal courts; records are at NARA (Philadelphia regional facility) and increasingly online via Ancestry, FamilySearch, and Fold3.

Passenger arrival lists (for immigrants arriving through Philadelphia or New York) are at NARA and searchable on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.

---

### 7. Land and Probate Records

- **Probate records (wills, inventories, guardianships):** Filed at the **county Register of Wills** from the colonial period. FamilySearch has a statewide collection: [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records and 446,607 images. Note that miners typically died with modest estates; wills are less common than for landowners, but administration and guardianship files can still appear.
- **Land/deed records:** County deed books at county courthouses. The Pennsylvania State Land Office (Harrisburg) holds original warrants, surveys, and patents ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)). Coal company land acquisitions may also document families displaced from farming.
- **Tax records:** Assessment lists and tax duplicates survive from the 1690s in some Pennsylvania counties and serve as census substitutes. Check county historical societies for pre-census tax lists.

---

### 8. Military Records

- Civil War (1861–1865) pension files and service records at NARA, searchable on Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) — many miners were Civil War veterans.
- Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- For immigrant miners who arrived after the Civil War, military records may be in the country of origin, not the U.S.

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

Mining town cemeteries were often segregated by ethnic parish. Two resources:
- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — crowdsourced headstone transcriptions, widely used for Pennsylvania coal region cemeteries.
- County historical societies often hold separate sexton records or burial registers not captured by Find A Grave.

---

### 10. Newspapers

Mining towns had active ethnic and English-language papers. **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) indexes many Pennsylvania titles. Local obituaries, mine accident notices, and immigrant community announcements in ethnic-language papers can be essential. The Pennsylvania State Library (Harrisburg) holds an extensive newspaper collection, including many ethnic-language titles.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|-----------|--------------|--------|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | Mine Inspector reports (1870+), naturalization records, state agency records, some company records | In-person; select records microfilmed |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**, Pottsville | Local church, mining company, and cemetery records for Schuylkill County | In-person |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum**, Scranton | Mining community records, labor records, immigrant community collections | In-person |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Lackawanna, Luzerne, and surrounding counties | By appointment |
| **Diocese of Allentown Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill, Carbon, and surrounding counties | By appointment |
| **County courthouses** | Marriage licenses, deeds, probate (Register of Wills) | In-person; many microfilmed |
| **NARA Philadelphia (National Archives)** | Federal court naturalizations, federal census originals, passenger lists | In-person; most records now on Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| **FamilySearch** ([familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)) | Census, marriage, probate collections; mine employment and accident image volumes; free | Online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, passenger lists, many state and county records | Subscription |

---

## Recommended Research Order

1. **Federal census 1870, 1880, 1900** — establish the family in a specific mining town and county; identify immigration year and origin
2. **Church records** for the appropriate ethnic parish — the only birth/death source for most of 1870–1905
3. **Mine Inspector Reports** (1870+) — if a family member died in a mine accident
4. **FamilySearch mining volumes** — Mine Worker Employment Cards for Schuylkill (indexed); Mine Accident Reports for Luzerne and Payroll Ledgers for Lackawanna (browse-only)
5. **County marriage records** via FamilySearch collections above
6. **Naturalization records** at county courts / Pennsylvania State Archives
7. **Passenger arrival lists** if the immigration date is known from census
8. **Pennsylvania Death Certificates (1906+)** for anyone who died after the statewide registration began — often names parents and birthplace

---

## Key Quirks to Keep in Mind

- **No statewide birth/death registration until 1906** — church records are your primary vital source for the entire late-1800s window.
- **Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878** — records for the Scranton and Carbondale area before that year are under Luzerne County. Search Luzerne County records first for pre-1878 events.
- **The 1890 federal census is destroyed** — no Pennsylvania state census exists to replace it for this decade.
- **Ethnic parish identification is critical** — knowing an ancestor's origin village narrows which parish they joined in Pennsylvania, since ethnic parishes were organized by national community and sometimes even by home region.
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne) and Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna) on FamilySearch are browse-only** — no name index exists; you must page through image by image.
- **Naturalization records before 1906 can be in any court** — check county courts of common pleas, not just federal courts.
- **The FamilySearch volume search returned 23 total volumes** for this region in 1860–1910; only the first page was retrieved. Browse the full list at FamilySearch for all counties to find additional record types not shown here.

# Massachusetts Early Colonial (c. 1620–1700) — Locality Research Guide

## Jurisdictional Context

**Standard place:** Massachusetts, United States  
**Target period:** c. 1620–1700 (Puritan settlement era)

Two **separate colonies** existed simultaneously and must be distinguished when searching:

- **Plymouth Colony (1620–1691)** — Founded by the Separatist Pilgrims. Towns include Plymouth, Duxbury, Scituate, Barnstable, Sandwich, Yarmouth, Taunton, Rehoboth, Marshfield, and Eastham. Its records are published and indexed **separately** from Massachusetts Bay Colony records.
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691)** — Dominated by Puritan reformers under Governor John Winthrop. The Great Migration (1630–1640) brought approximately 20,000 settlers. (Wikipedia: [Massachusetts Bay Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony))
- **Province of Massachusetts Bay (1691–)** — The Crown merged Plymouth Colony, Massachusetts Bay Colony, Maine, and Nova Scotia into a single royal province in 1691.

**County formation:** Massachusetts established four original counties in **1643** — Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk (original; dissolved 1679, reconstituted 1793), and Suffolk. Deeds and probate records are organized at the county level from 1643 onward.

**Maine:** Was part of Massachusetts until statehood in 1820. Early Maine families may have Massachusetts-held records.

**Registration levels (critical distinction):**
- **Town-level** vital recording was mandated by the General Court in **1639** — making Massachusetts one of the earliest civil registration jurisdictions in North America. (FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Statewide** vital registration did not begin until **1841** — more than 200 years later.
- **No federal census** exists for this period; the first was 1790.

> ⚠️ There is no census record source for any family in the 1620–1700 window. Research depends entirely on town, church, court, land, and probate records.

---

## Records Available

### 1. Town Vital Records — 🟢 Indexed + Images on FamilySearch
The most important starting point for this period.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890*  
Collection ID: [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) · 3,456,789 records

Town clerks were ordered to record births, marriages, and deaths from **1639**. The **Tanner–Corbin series** (*Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850*) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is the standard published reference for colonial vital events. Many volumes are freely accessible at the Internet Archive and via NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org). (FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

**Coverage gap:** Not every event was recorded; early town books are sometimes incomplete or lost. When a vital record is missing, go directly to church records.

---

### 2. Church Records (Congregational) — 🟢 Indexed + Images on FamilySearch
As the established church of the colony, Congregational meetings maintained **membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary records** (excommunications, admonishments). These frequently document events that never appeared in the town book.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920*  
Collection ID: [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) · 987,654 records

Many early church records have also been published in the *Colonial Society of Massachusetts* series and in local historical society volumes. (FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))

**Repository for unpublished early church records:** Congregational Library & Archives, 14 Beacon St., Boston.

---

### 3. Probate Records — 🟢 Indexed + Images on FamilySearch
County-level probate courts recorded wills, inventories, guardianships, and estate administrations from the **1630s** onward. Probate files routinely name spouses, children, and other heirs — making them one of the richest sources for reconstructing family relationships when direct vital evidence is absent.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991*  
Collection ID: [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) · 567,890 records

**Repositories:** County probate courts (originals); Massachusetts Archives (colonial-era records); FamilySearch (digitized).

---

### 4. Land Records (Deeds) — 🟡 Partial Microfilm; Physical Holdings
Land records were recorded at the **county level from the 1630s** and survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds. Colonial-era land grants from the General Court are held at the Massachusetts Archives. (FamilySearch Wiki: [Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

**Repositories:** County Registries of Deeds (originals); Massachusetts Archives (colonial grants); FamilySearch (partial microfilm).

---

### 5. Colonial Court Records — 🔴 Physical / Microfilm
The General Court, county courts, and inferior courts generated civil suits, criminal cases, and administrative matters that name family members, ages, and residences. These are especially valuable when no vital or church record survives.

**Repository:** Massachusetts Archives, 220 Morrissey Blvd., Boston (holds original colony and court records from the 1620s onward).

---

### 6. Plymouth Colony Records (1620–1691) — 🟢 Published and Indexed (Separately)
Plymouth Colony is a **separate jurisdiction** — its records do not overlap with Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Determine which colony your ancestor lived in **before** choosing a record series.

Key published resources:
- *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England* (Nathaniel Shurtleff, ed., 12 vols.)
- *The Mayflower Descendant* (NEHGS periodical, ongoing)
- Pilgrim Hall Museum (Plymouth) and Plimoth Patuxent hold original and reproduced Plymouth materials

---

### 7. Great Migration Study Materials — 🟢 Essential Published Reference
The **Great Migration Study Project** (New England Historic Genealogical Society) produced multi-volume biographical sketches of every known settler who arrived in New England 1620–1643, compiled by Robert Charles Anderson. This is the standard starting point for any Puritan ancestor. It synthesizes town records, church records, court records, English origins, and published genealogies into one searchable resource.

**Access:** NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org, subscription); physical copies at major genealogical libraries.

---

### 8. Military Records — 🟡 Published / State Archives / Fold3
Early colonial conflicts — including King Philip's War (1675–1676) — are documented in published muster rolls and at the Massachusetts Archives. Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) holds some colonial-era records. Federal military records (NARA) do not begin until the Revolutionary War era and are **not relevant** to this period.

---

### 9. Cemetery Records — 🟡 Find A Grave; Physical Sites
Early colonial burying grounds exist throughout Massachusetts. Find A Grave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has indexed many surviving markers. Be aware that many 17th-century graves are unmarked or have lost their stones entirely.

---

### 10. Passenger Lists (1620–1700 arrivals) — ⚠️ No systematic records survive
FamilySearch's *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (Collection ID 1784312) covers only **post-target period** arrivals and is not useful for 1600s research. For colonial-era arrivals, consult the Great Migration volumes and English parish records of origin. NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)) holds later federal-era immigration material only.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Holdings for This Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Colony records, General Court records, colonial court files, land grants — from 1620s | In-person; some digitized |
| **NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org** (Boston) | Great Migration study, manuscript collections, published genealogies, Mayflower materials | In-person + subscription online |
| **FamilySearch** | Town vital records (1620–1890), church records (1630–1920), probate records (1635–1991) | Free online |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Land/deed records from 1630s | In-person; some county websites |
| **County Probate Courts** | Probate files from 1630s | In-person; digitized on FamilySearch |
| **Congregational Library & Archives** (Boston) | Early Congregational church records not yet on FamilySearch | In-person |
| **American Antiquarian Society** (Worcester) | Early printed colonial histories, newspapers, pamphlets | In-person by appointment |
| **Pilgrim Hall Museum / Plimoth Patuxent** | Plymouth Colony records, Pilgrim documents | In-person; some online |
| **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)) | No colonial-era records; federal records post-1776 only for this region | Online + in-person |

---

## Quirks and Cautions

1. **Plymouth Colony ≠ Massachusetts Bay Colony.** These are separate jurisdictions with entirely separate record series. Identify which colony first.
2. **Town-level registration (1639) vs. statewide (1841).** For the 1600s, you need town and church records — not state vital records.
3. **No census for this period.** The first federal census was 1790; no colonial-era census exists.
4. **Original Norfolk County (1643–1679)** was dissolved; its towns shifted to Essex and Suffolk counties. Records from this era may be catalogued under the earlier county.
5. **Secretary hand.** Original 17th-century documents use archaic handwriting styles (secretary hand, mixed hand) that require paleographic skills to read.

# Massachusetts Early Colonial (c. 1620–1700) — Locality Research Guide

## Jurisdictional Context

**Two separate colonies** coexisted and must be distinguished at the outset:

| Colony | Years | Key Towns | Records |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620–1691 | Plymouth, Duxbury, Scituate, Barnstable, Yarmouth, Taunton, Rehoboth, Eastham | Published and indexed **separately** |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1628–1691 | Boston, Salem, Cambridge, Watertown, Roxbury, Newbury, Ipswich, Springfield | Separate record series |
| **Province of Massachusetts Bay** | 1691 onward | All of the above + Maine + Nova Scotia | Merged royal province |

**Counties formed 1643:** Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk (original; dissolved 1679, reconstituted 1793), Suffolk. Deeds and probate are organized at the county level.

**Registration levels — a critical distinction:**
- **Town-level** vital recording mandated by the General Court **1639** — one of the earliest civil registration mandates in North America ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Statewide** registration did not begin until **1841** — more than 200 years later
- **No federal census** before 1790 — there are *no census records* for this period

---

## Records Available

### 1. 🟢 Town Vital Records — Indexed + Images on FamilySearch
**The primary starting point.** Town clerks recorded births, marriages, and deaths from 1639.

- **FamilySearch:** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) (Collection 2061550) — 3,456,789 records
- **Tanner–Corbin series** (*Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850*): published abstracts of over 200 Massachusetts town clerk books — the standard colonial-era reference. Many volumes are free at the Internet Archive and NEHGS.
- **Gap:** Early books are sometimes incomplete or lost. When a vital record is missing, go directly to church records.

---

### 2. 🟢 Church Records (Congregational) — Indexed + Images on FamilySearch
As the established church of the colony, Congregational meetings maintained **membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings** (excommunications, admonishments) — often capturing events that never appeared in the town book.

- **FamilySearch:** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) (Collection 1921657) — 987,654 records
- Many early records also published in the *Colonial Society of Massachusetts* series and local historical society volumes ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Unpublished early records:** Congregational Library & Archives, 14 Beacon St., Boston

---

### 3. 🟢 Probate Records — Indexed + Images on FamilySearch
County-level probate courts recorded wills, inventories, guardianships, and estate administrations from the **1630s** onward. Probate files routinely name spouses, children, and other heirs — often the richest source for reconstructing family relationships.

- **FamilySearch:** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) (Collection 1678901) — 567,890 records
- **Repositories:** County probate courts (originals); Massachusetts Archives (colonial-era); FamilySearch (digitized)

---

### 4. 🟡 Land Records (Deeds) — Partial Microfilm; Physical Holdings
Recorded at the county level from the **1630s** in complete runs at county registries of deeds. Colonial land grants from the General Court are at the Massachusetts Archives. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

- **Repositories:** County Registries of Deeds (originals); Massachusetts Archives (colonial grants); FamilySearch (partial microfilm)

---

### 5. 🔴 Colonial Court Records — Physical / Microfilm
The General Court, county courts, and inferior courts produced civil and criminal files naming family members, ages, and residences — especially valuable when no vital or church record survives.

- **Repository:** Massachusetts Archives, 220 Morrissey Blvd., Boston — holds original colony and court records from the 1620s onward

---

### 6. 🟢 Plymouth Colony Records (1620–1691) — Published and Indexed (Separately)
Plymouth Colony is a **completely separate jurisdiction** from Massachusetts Bay Colony. Its records do not overlap. Determine which colony your ancestor lived in before choosing which series to search.

- *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England* (Nathaniel Shurtleff, ed., 12 vols.)
- *The Mayflower Descendant* (NEHGS periodical)
- Pilgrim Hall Museum (Plymouth) and Plimoth Patuxent

---

### 7. 🟢 Great Migration Study — Essential Published Reference
The **Great Migration Study Project** (NEHGS, compiled by Robert Charles Anderson) produced multi-volume biographical sketches of every known settler who arrived in New England 1620–1643, synthesizing town, church, court, and English-origin records. **This is the essential starting point for any Puritan family.**

- **Access:** [AmericanAncestors.org](https://www.americanancestors.org) (subscription); physical copies at major genealogical libraries

---

### 8. 🟡 Military Records — Published / State Archives / Fold3
Early colonial conflicts, including **King Philip's War (1675–1676)**, are documented in published muster rolls and at the Massachusetts Archives. [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com) holds some colonial-era material. Federal NARA military records do not cover the colonial period.

---

### 9. 🟡 Cemetery Records — Find A Grave; Physical Sites
Early colonial burying grounds exist throughout Massachusetts. [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com) has indexed many surviving markers. Many 17th-century graves are unmarked or have lost their stones.

---

### ⚠️ What Does NOT Apply to This Period
| Record Type | Why It Doesn't Apply |
|---|---|
| Federal census | First census was 1790 |
| FamilySearch Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (Collection 1784312) | Entirely post-target period |
| FamilySearch Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (Collection 1459213) | Entirely post-target period |
| NARA federal military records | Cover Revolutionary War era onward only |
| Statewide vital registration | Didn't begin until 1841 |

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Colony records, General Court records, court files, land grants — from 1620s | In-person; some digitized |
| **NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org** | Great Migration study, manuscripts, published genealogies, Mayflower materials | In-person + subscription online |
| **FamilySearch** | Town vital records (1620–1890), church records (1630–1920), probate (1635–1991) | Free online |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Land/deed records from 1630s | In-person; some county websites |
| **Congregational Library & Archives** (Boston) | Early Congregational church records | In-person |
| **American Antiquarian Society** (Worcester) | Early printed colonial histories, pamphlets, newspapers | In-person by appointment |
| **Pilgrim Hall Museum / Plimoth Patuxent** | Plymouth Colony records | In-person; some online |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal records only — not relevant for 1620–1700 | Online + in-person |

---

## Key Quirks to Know Before You Search

1. **Plymouth Colony ≠ Massachusetts Bay Colony.** Separate jurisdictions, entirely separate record series. Identify which colony first.
2. **Town registration 1639, statewide 1841.** Always use town and church records for this era — not state vital records.
3. **No census for this period.** Your entire research framework rests on town, church, court, land, and probate records.
4. **Original Norfolk County (1643–1679)** was dissolved; its towns shifted to Essex and Suffolk. Check both county series.
5. **Secretary hand.** Original 17th-century documents use archaic script styles — consider paleographic assistance.
6. **Maine families** with colonial roots will have Massachusetts-held records (Maine was part of Massachusetts until 1820).
7. **Great Migration volumes first.** If your ancestor arrived 1620–1643, Robert Charles Anderson's NEHGS series is the single most efficient entry point before you begin searching individual record collections.

# Oklahoma Territory — Land Run Era Locality Guide
**Period: 1889–1907**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

The Land Run of **April 22, 1889** opened the "Unassigned Lands" of central Oklahoma, but formal territorial organization didn't follow until the **Organic Act of May 2, 1890**, which created **Oklahoma Territory** (capital: Guthrie). The eastern portion remained **Indian Territory** throughout this period — home to the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole) — with entirely separate civil and federal record-keeping under tribal and Bureau of Indian Affairs authority.

Both territories merged into the **State of Oklahoma on November 16, 1907**.

> **Critical split:** Which jurisdiction's records apply depends on *where within the territory the event occurred* — western Oklahoma (Oklahoma Territory) vs. eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory). When location is uncertain, search both sides.

---

## 🏆 Land Records — Prime Source for This Era

Every settler who filed a homestead claim generated federal paperwork. This is the single most important record class for Land Run families.

- **FamilySearch collection 1541872** — *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907*: 234,567 indexed records with 117,283 images. **Digitization level: indexed + images.** → [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)
- **BLM General Land Office Records** at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free online search of land patents with downloadable document images.
- **NARA Record Group 49** (General Land Office), Washington DC — full homestead case files: original application, proof of settlement with **named witnesses**, and final patent. Rejected applications also survive and frequently contain family details.

Each homestead file typically names the claimant, may name neighbors as witnesses, gives age, occupation, and prior residence. *(FamilySearch Wiki: [Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run))*

---

## 📊 Census Records

| Census | Notes | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory special census** | Uniquely survives — most 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire. Captures the very first Land Run settlers. | Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City |
| **1900 Federal Census** | Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory enumerated **separately** | FamilySearch, NARA |
| **1910 Federal Census** | First census of the unified state | FamilySearch, NARA |

---

## ⚠️ Vital Records — Major Gap for 1889–1907

Oklahoma **statewide** vital registration did not begin until **October 1908**, and compliance was poor until the 1930s. **No civil birth or death records exist for the entire 1889–1907 territorial period.** *(FamilySearch Wiki: [Oklahoma Vital Records — Registration History](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Registration_History))*

**Substitute sources for births and deaths:**
- Church registers (Baptist, Methodist, and Catholic congregations began establishing congregations sporadically from 1889)
- Territorial census schedules (name, age, relationships)
- Cemetery records (Find A Grave; Oklahoma Historical Society holdings)
- Newspaper birth/death notices (Newspapers.com; Oklahoma Historical Society newspaper collection)

---

## 💒 Marriage Records

County-level marriage registration began with county organization from 1890.

- **FamilySearch collection 2134789** — *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995*: 456,789 records covering 913,578 persons, with 228,394 images. **Digitization level: indexed + images.** → [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)

---

## ⛪ Church and Mission Records

The primary substitute for civil vital registration in this era.

- **FamilySearch collection 1654321** — *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965*: 123,456 records with 61,728 images. **Digitization level: indexed + images.** → [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)
- **Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives** — historical parish registers
- **Diocese of Oklahoma City** — Catholic parish registers

*(FamilySearch Wiki: [Oklahoma Vital Records — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Repositories))*

---

## 🏛️ Territorial Court Records (1890–1907)

District court records include civil and criminal cases, probate files, naturalization petitions (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record), and county tax rolls documenting early settlers.

- **Primary repository:** National Archives at Fort Worth, TX
- **Also:** Oklahoma State Archives

*(FamilySearch Wiki: [Oklahoma Territorial Records — Courts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))*

---

## 🪶 Indian Territory — Dawes Commission Rolls

Essential for families in eastern Oklahoma or anyone with Native American ancestry among the Five Civilized Tribes.

- **Dawes Commission Rolls (1898–1914)**: documented tribal citizenship for the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole nations.
- **FamilySearch collection 1987432** — *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959*: 567,890 records with 283,945 images. **Digitization level: indexed + images.** → [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)
- Bureau of Indian Affairs records also held at NARA.

---

## 🪖 Military, 📰 Newspapers, ⚰️ Cemetery Records

| Type | Source | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Military service & pensions | Fold3; NARA Washington DC | Subscription / in-person |
| Historical newspapers | Newspapers.com; Oklahoma Historical Society | Subscription / in-person |
| Cemetery | Find A Grave; Oklahoma Historical Society | Free online / in-person |

> **Newspapers are especially valuable here.** Dozens of new-town papers were founded in 1889–1890 immediately after the Land Run and recorded arrivals, land claims, and vital events long before civil registration existed.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Oklahoma Historical Society**, Oklahoma City | 1890 territorial census, land run claim files, town lot records, early county records, newspapers |
| **Oklahoma State Archives**, Oklahoma City | Birth/death records from 1908 onward; territorial records |
| **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** | Territorial court records (1890–1907) |
| **National Archives, Washington DC** | Land records (RG 49), military records |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Land patents — glorecords.blm.gov (free, online) |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections: land, marriages, church, Indian rolls |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1900, 1910) — subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records — subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers — subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records — free |

---

## Research Quirks & Warnings

1. **The Land Run predates the Territory.** The Run of April 22, 1889 predates formal Oklahoma Territory by nearly a year (Organic Act: May 2, 1890). Territorial records begin May 1890; the period April–May 1889 has no territorial record infrastructure.

2. **Two-jurisdiction split.** Records for 1889–1907 are split between Oklahoma Territory (west) and Indian Territory (east). If the family's precise location is unknown, search both sides.

3. **No civil vital records before October 1908.** Statewide registration began then, but compliance was poor until the 1930s. Use church records, census, cemetery records, and newspapers as substitutes for the entire territorial period.

4. **The 1890 Oklahoma Territory census uniquely survives.** Most of the 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire; this special census (held at the Oklahoma Historical Society) is the only snapshot of the very first Land Run settlers.

5. **Trace origins in departure states.** Land Run families commonly came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri. Tracing their origins requires searching those states' records before 1889.

6. **County formation dates matter.** County records begin only after a county was formally organized. Verify when your specific county was created — it determines when local vital and court records start.

7. **Indian Territory had entirely separate record-keeping.** The Dawes Commission Rolls (1898–1914) are essential for Native American ancestry and for anyone whose family settled in eastern Oklahoma.

---

*Note: The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Oklahoma-specific place pages through the automated tool; the guidance above is grounded in targeted wiki searches returning content from the Oklahoma Land Records, Oklahoma Vital Records, and Oklahoma Territorial Records wiki pages. Visit those pages directly for the most current coverage details.*

## Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, ca. 1800 (Pre-Statehood / Territorial Period)

**Place:** Present-day Alabama, United States
**Period:** c. 1790–1819 (pre-statehood, primarily Mississippi Territory era)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Alabama around 1800 does not exist as a single jurisdiction — it is a patchwork of overlapping authorities, and that directly determines where records are filed and who created them.

| Period | Governing authority | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French colony | Mobile area only |
| 1763–1780 | British colony | Mobile and coast |
| 1780–1798/1813 | Spanish colonial (Mobile District) | Mobile held by Spain until 1813; rest of area disputed |
| **1798–1817** | **Mississippi Territory** | **Present-day Alabama's primary records jurisdiction ca. 1800** |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | Carved from Mississippi Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | Statehood Dec. 14, 1819 |

**At ca. 1800, the Mississippi Territory (established 1798) governs the American-administered portion.** The Mobile area southwest corner remained under Spanish control until 1813 — two separate record-creating authorities operated simultaneously in the same region. Washington County, formed in 1800, was the first county organized within present-day Alabama under the Territory. Most of northern Alabama had no organized county government until after 1805; the Creek and Cherokee nations held much of it.

**Critical filing quirk:** FamilySearch organizes records at the state level. Pre-statehood Alabama records created under the Mississippi Territory are filed under **"Mississippi, United States"** scope, not under Alabama. You must search both Alabama and Mississippi collections on FamilySearch for this period.

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

#### 1. Census and Census Substitutes ★ Prime source for ca. 1800

**What exists:** The Mississippi Territory conducted its own censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**, enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki page "Alabama Genealogy" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these territorial censuses are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery.

The **1810 federal census** is the first federal enumeration to cover present-day Alabama (then still Mississippi Territory). The **1800 federal census** covered the Mississippi Territory's original southern strip, but much of present-day northern Alabama was outside U.S. jurisdiction at that time — don't assume 1800 federal coverage for the whole region.

**FamilySearch collections (overlapping this period):**
- **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection 2016756) — 287,634 records; **0 images** (index only, no browsable scans) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)
- **Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890** (collection 1927171) — 198,340 records; **0 images** (index only) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171)

**Tax lists and militia rolls** served as census substitutes in years without enumeration. These are held primarily at ADAH; digitization status on FamilySearch is a gap (no volumes returned for this period — see §9 below).

**Digitization level: Index-only on FamilySearch. No browsable images available through FamilySearch for this period.**

---

#### 2. Land Records ★ Richest and most consistent source

**What exists:** Land is the one record class guaranteed to document nearly every adult male settler. Three overlapping series apply:

- **Spanish land grants** (Mobile area, pre-1813): Claims by families in the Mobile District under Spanish authority. Held at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville — per the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Federal land entry files** (post-1807): The U.S. began selling public land in present-day Alabama through the St. Stephens Land Office (1807). Federal patents from this date forward are fully searchable and **browsable as digitized images** at the **BLM General Land Office website** ([https://glorecords.blm.gov/](https://glorecords.blm.gov/)).
- **Mississippi Territory court-confirmed claims**: Pre-existing British/Spanish grants that settlers had confirmed through territorial courts — filed under the Mississippi Territory land records series.

**FamilySearch collection (Mississippi/territorial scope):**
- **Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907** (collection 1919694) — 312,450 records, **156,225 images** — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694)

**Digitization level: Images available on FamilySearch for the Mississippi/territorial series; BLM GLO fully digitized and freely browsable for federal patents from 1807.**

---

#### 3. Court Records

**What exists:** The territorial courts of Washington County (est. 1800) and later Madison County (est. 1808) created the first local court records in present-day Alabama. These include civil suits, criminal cases, and early probate proceedings.

**FamilySearch collection:**
- **Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920** (collection 1855293) — 245,670 records, **122,835 images** — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855295)

**Digitization level: Images available on FamilySearch under the Mississippi scope.**

---

#### 4. Church Records

**What exists:** No civil vital registration existed anywhere in Alabama in this period (statewide registration did not begin until 1908). Church registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are the only vital event records for most families. Catholic registers are especially important for the Mobile area and its Spanish/French-period settlements.

**FamilySearch collections:**
- **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection 1986396) — 156,789 records, **78,394 images** — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)
- **Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950** (collection 2034891) — 87,654 records, **43,827 images** — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891)

**Digitization level: Images available on FamilySearch. Note that the Alabama church collection starts only in 1803.**

---

#### 5. Colonial Records — Mobile Area (Spanish and French)

For families in or near Mobile, the genealogical trail runs through European archives, not American ones.

**Spanish colonial records (1780–1813):** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), the Mobile District records include census returns, Catholic church registers, and land grants. Primary repository: **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain**. Copies held at the **Library of Congress**, Washington, D.C.

**French colonial records (1702–1763):** Held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm copies at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**.

**Digitization level: Physical/microfilm only for most colonial materials. Some ANOM and AGI materials have been partially digitized on their respective institutional portals, but access is not consolidated through FamilySearch.**

---

#### 6. Marriage Records

**FamilySearch collection:**
- **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection 1598408) — 612,345 records, **306,172 images** — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)

**Note:** This collection starts in **1809** — the very end of the Mississippi Territory era. For marriages before 1809 in present-day Alabama, church registers (§4 above) and territorial court records (§3) are the only sources.

**Digitization level: Images available on FamilySearch, but coverage for the pre-statehood window is limited to 1809–1819.**

---

#### 7. Probate Records

**FamilySearch collection:**
- **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (collection 1537764) — 438,210 records, **219,105 images** — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764)

**Note:** Like marriages, Alabama probate coverage starts in 1809. Earlier estate proceedings (pre-1809) would be in Washington County or territorial court records under the Mississippi scope.

---

#### 8. Military Records

**What exists:**
- **Creek War of 1813–1814**: Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at the National Archives. Available through Fold3 ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)).
- **War of 1812**: Alabama territorial militia participated; records at National Archives and ADAH.
- **Territorial militia rolls** (pre-1813): Held at ADAH; document male settlers outside census years.

**Digitization level: Pension files at NARA are partially digitized via Fold3. Territorial militia rolls at ADAH — physical/microfilm, not browsed through FamilySearch.**

---

#### 9. Digitized Browsable Volumes — Direct Answer to Your Question

You asked specifically about digitized, browsable volumes. **FamilySearch's volume_search returned zero results for Alabama across the entire 1790–1825 window**, even when filtering specifically for land, census, tax, court, probate, military, and religious record types. This is a genuine coverage gap on FamilySearch: no image groups (microfilm rolls / book scans) are indexed for this territory and period in FamilySearch's Records Management Service.

**Where browsable digitized volumes do exist for this period:**

| Source | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **BLM GLO** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov/)) | Federal land patents, Alabama from 1807; fully browsable by name or county | Free, no login |
| **ADAH Digital Collections** ([digital.archives.alabama.gov](https://digital.archives.alabama.gov/)) | Territorial records, early county records, maps — browse by collection | Free |
| **FamilySearch Catalog** | Microfilm reels digitized for Washington County, Baldwin County territorial records may appear as unindexed image groups in the Catalog (separate from the Records search) | Free; search under "Alabama" → county in the Catalog |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1810 federal census (images + index); some territorial-era compiled records | Subscription |
| **Library of Congress / Chronicling America** | Early Alabama newspapers from the territorial period | Free |

The FamilySearch **Catalog** (separate from the Records search engine) is the best place to look for browse-only microfilm digitizations — search under **Alabama > [county name]** in the Catalog to find film rolls that may have been digitized but not indexed.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery | Territorial censuses, militia rolls, county records, maps, early state records | On-site; digital.archives.alabama.gov online |
| **National Archives, Southeast Region (Atlanta)** | Federal territorial records, military pensions, land entry files | On-site; NARA online |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville** | Spanish colonial Mobile District records | On-site; partial digitization at pares.mcu.es |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence** | French colonial records | On-site; partial digitization at archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish colonial records, early maps | On-site; many items at loc.gov |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Local records, colonial microfilm | On-site |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents from 1807 | Free online: glorecords.blm.gov |

---

### Research Quirks and Gotchas

1. **Search both Alabama AND Mississippi on FamilySearch.** Records created in present-day Alabama under the Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) are filed under the *Mississippi* scope in FamilySearch collections. If you search only Alabama, you will miss most pre-1809 records.

2. **Mobile had a separate colonial jurisdiction until 1813.** Families in the Mobile area before 1813 are in Spanish colonial records (Seville / Library of Congress), not in American territorial records. Don't assume a Mobile family's early vital or land records exist in U.S. repositories.

3. **No Alabama county existed before 1800.** Washington County was the first (1800). For events in present-day Alabama before 1800 outside the Mobile area, there is essentially no local record-creating authority — Spanish grants and French/Spanish church registers are all that exist.

4. **No statewide vital registration until 1908.** There is no civil birth, marriage, or death registration for this period anywhere in Alabama. Church registers and territorial court filings are the only substitutes.

5. **Federal land sales began 1807.** Before that date, only confirmed Spanish/British grantees and squatters appear in land records. Post-1807 public land sales through the St. Stephens Land Office are the first widespread federal documentation of settlers.

6. **The 1810 federal census is the first to cover all of present-day Alabama** as Mississippi Territory. The 1800 federal census covered the territory's original southern strip only — much of present-day northern Alabama was not enumerated.

7. **FamilySearch volume_search found no digitized image groups for Alabama 1790–1825.** For browsable scans, go to ADAH's digital collections portal and the FamilySearch Catalog directly, rather than Records search.

8. **Creek War displacement (1813–1814) fractured records.** The Creek War drove out many settlers and disrupted county government. Some early county records were lost during this period.

---

### Summary: What to Search First

For a settler in present-day Alabama around 1800, the priority order is:

1. **Land records** under the Mississippi scope on FamilySearch (collection 1919694), plus BLM GLO for post-1807 patents
2. **Mississippi Territory census substitutes** on FamilySearch (collection 1927171) and request ADAH copies of the 1801/1805/1808 territorial censuses
3. **1810 federal census** (first federal coverage of the whole region)
4. **Church records** under both Alabama (collection 1986396) and Mississippi (collection 2034891) scopes
5. **Court records** under the Mississippi scope (collection 1855293)
6. **ADAH digital collections** for browsable territorial-era volumes not indexed on FamilySearch
7. **Spanish colonial records** if the family was in the Mobile area before 1813

## Locality Research Guide — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region
### Schuylkill · Luzerne · Carbon · Lackawanna · Northumberland Counties, 1860–1890
*Focus: Irish immigrant miners*

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**The five core anthracite counties** occupy northeastern and east-central Pennsylvania. Their genealogical quirks are inseparable from the coal industry that shaped them:

| County | Formed | From | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill | 1811 | Berks & Northumberland | Pottsville is county seat; southern anthracite field |
| Luzerne | 1786 | Northumberland | Wilkes-Barre is county seat; Wyoming Valley field |
| Carbon | 1843 | Northampton & Monroe | Mauch Chunk (now Jim Thorpe); Lehigh Valley coal |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878** | **Luzerne** | Scranton area; **records before 1878 are in Luzerne** |
| Northumberland | 1772 | Lancaster, Berks, Bedford, Northampton, Cumberland | Sunbury seat; Shamokin coal patch |

> ⚠️ **Critical boundary quirk:** Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878. Any event in the Scranton/Carbondale area before that date — birth, marriage, naturalization, probate — was recorded under **Luzerne County**. Always search Luzerne first for Lackawanna families before 1878.

**Population scale (Schuylkill, the largest anthracite county):**
89,510 (1860) → 116,428 (1870) → 129,974 (1880) — a 45% surge driven almost entirely by mine labor immigration. Luzerne was comparable or larger.

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

#### 🏛️ Vital Records — Civil Registration
**⚠️ Gap: Pennsylvania statewide vital registration did not begin until 1906.** For 1860–1890, there are no statewide birth or death certificates. You must rely on church registers, census mortality schedules, and funeral home records as substitutes.

Some Pennsylvania counties began local registration earlier under an 1852 act, but compliance was sporadic and coverage in the coal counties was thin. Do not assume a civil vital record exists for this period — check for it at the county courthouse, but treat church records as the primary source.

---

#### ⛪ Church Records — **PRIMARY SOURCE for 1860–1890 vital events**
For Irish Catholic miners, the Catholic parish register is the most important record class in the region. The major Irish parishes include:
- **St. Patrick's** (Pottsville, Schuylkill Co.) — serving Irish miners from the 1830s
- **St. Canisius, St. Rose of Lima** and other parishes in Wilkes-Barre / Scranton / Carbondale (Luzerne/Lackawanna)
- Numerous company-town parishes established by mining corporations

**FamilySearch holdings (Schuylkill County):**
- Image group **007936751** — Church Records, 1842–1895, 187 images — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image by image. Records are in **English and German** — German Lutheran and Reformed congregations are included alongside Irish Catholic ones.

The wiki confirms that the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) holds additional church records not yet digitized. Diocese of Allentown archives hold Schuylkill and Carbon County Catholic records; Diocese of Scranton archives hold Lackawanna and Luzerne records.

---

#### 📋 Census Records
Federal census enumerations are fully available and name-indexed for this region:

| Census Year | Value for Irish Miners | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1860 | Names, ages, birthplaces | Irish-born listed; no relationship column |
| 1870 | First to record parents' birthplaces for children | Key for confirming Irish origin |
| 1880 | Relationship to household head added | Most genealogically rich pre-1900 census |
| **1890** | **Mostly destroyed in 1921 fire** | **Only fragments survive** — treat as absent |
| 1900 | Month/year of birth; years in U.S.; citizenship status | Not in your window but a critical bridge |

> The 1880 census mortality schedules record deaths in the year June 1879–May 1880 — include occupation and birthplace and are available on FamilySearch.

Pennsylvania is covered in all federal censuses 1790–1940. The 1890 destruction is a significant gap — bridge it with church records, city directories, and naturalization papers.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Pennsylvania Genealogy, Census Records section: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records)*

---

#### ⚖️ Naturalization Records — **HIGH PRIORITY for Irish miners**
These are among the richest sources for Irish origins. They record country (and sometimes county) of birth, date and port of arrival, and sometimes the names of witnesses (often relatives or neighbors).

**FamilySearch holdings (Schuylkill County):**
- Image group **007936750** — Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed page by page.

**Pre-1906 structure:** Before September 27, 1906, naturalization could happen in *any court of record* — Quarter Sessions Court, Court of Common Pleas, and Orphans' Court all had jurisdiction. A miner might have filed a Declaration of Intent ("first papers") in one county and completed his Petition in another. Search all three court series in each county.

**Post-1906:** Naturalization centralized in federal courts. For eastern Pennsylvania, records after 1906 are at **NARA Philadelphia** (now NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia).

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Pennsylvania Naturalization Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records)*

---

#### 💒 Marriage Records
**FamilySearch holdings (Schuylkill County):**
- Image group **007936753** — Marriage Records, 1870–1910, 94 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed). Note this volume begins at 1870; earlier marriages in the target period will not be here.

Marriage licenses in Pennsylvania were filed at the county courthouse. Before the license requirement took effect statewide, marriages were recorded primarily in church registers.

---

#### 🏠 Probate Records
**FamilySearch holdings (Schuylkill County):**
- Image group **007936749** — Probate Records, 1851–1930, 412 images — **browse-only** (0% indexed).
- **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) — 2,304,118 images statewide, covering all counties. This is the main digitized probate resource.

Probate records (wills, estate inventories, letters of administration) can name children, widows, and siblings. Even a miner with little property often appears in administration papers.

---

#### 📜 Deed Records
**FamilySearch holdings (Schuylkill County):**
- Image group **007936752** — Deed Records, 1815–1900, 543 images — **partially indexed** (22% name-searchable). Worth running a name search, but also browse the unindexed portion.

Miners renting company housing won't appear in deed books, but those who bought land or a town lot will. Deed grantee/grantor indexes at the county courthouse are the most complete finding aid.

---

#### ⛏️ Coal Mining Records — **SPECIALIZED SOURCE, unique to this region**
This is the record class that sets the anthracite region apart from most other research areas.

**Colliery payroll ledgers and employment records:** Where they survive, these list worker names, nationalities, job classification (miner, laborer, door boy), and sometimes prior residence or next of kin. The **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) holds payroll ledgers for several collieries. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, Coal Mining Records section: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Coal_Mining_Records)*

**Mine accident and coroner records:** Mining was lethal. Coroner's inquest records for mine deaths frequently record the deceased's name, age, birthplace, and surviving family. Check county coroner records at each courthouse and at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

**Pennsylvania Bureau of Mines annual reports (1870 onward):** Published lists of fatal mine accidents by colliery, sometimes naming the victim and cause of death. Held at the Pennsylvania State Library and digitized at HathiTrust.

---

#### ☘️ Molly Maguires Records — **UNIQUE Irish-specific source**
The Molly Maguires, a secret fraternal organization active among Irish miners in Schuylkill and surrounding counties during the 1860s–1870s, generated a body of records with no parallel elsewhere:

- **Trial transcripts and court records** from the 1875–1877 prosecutions name hundreds of Irish-born miners and their associates.
- **Pinkerton detective reports** (James McParland's infiltration) are held at the Library of Congress and in published editions — they name individuals, describe family connections, and identify home townlands in Ireland for some subjects.
- **Newspaper coverage** in the *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville) is extensive and names many participants.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, Molly Maguires section: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires)*

Even if your ancestor wasn't a Molly Maguire, these records can establish neighborhood and community networks connecting Irish families across the region.

---

#### 🪖 Military Records
Many Irish miners served in the Civil War (1861–1865) — just before your window opens. Pennsylvania raised more than 360 regiments. Military records to check:

- **Federal service records and pension files** at NARA — pensions especially are rich (list age, birthplace, physical description, widow/children).
- **Pennsylvania Civil War Veterans' Card File** at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) — indexed.
- The 48th Pennsylvania Infantry recruited heavily from Schuylkill County miners, including many Irish-born. It performed the famous "Crater" mine explosion at Petersburg in 1864 — its muster rolls and regimental history are well documented.

---

#### 🛳️ Immigration & Passenger Lists
Irish miners arriving 1845–1870 typically landed at:
- **Philadelphia** (primary port for many from Munster and Connacht)
- **New York / Castle Garden** (for Ulster and Leinster arrivals and post-1855 traffic)

Passenger lists 1820–1891 are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Search by name, approximate year, and origin port. Note that many migrants came via Liverpool regardless of Irish county of origin — filter by departure port as well as arrival.

---

#### 📰 Newspapers
The **Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, 1825–present) is the paper of record for the southern anthracite field. It covered deaths, marriages, accidents, community events, and Molly Maguires trials in granular detail. Historical issues are partially digitized at **Newspapers.com** and **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress). The Schuylkill County Historical Society holds print runs.

For Luzerne/Lackawanna: the **Scranton Republican** and **Wilkes-Barre Record** served the Wyoming Valley field.

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |

| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Probate collection 1999196 (2.3M images); Schuylkill naturalization, church, marriage, deed volumes (browse-only) | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses (all years); PA statewide collections | Subscription |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Colliery payrolls, local newspapers, church records, county histories | In-person / some online |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Bureau reports; Civil War veterans file; county records on microfilm | In-person / some online |
| **NARA Mid-Atlantic** (Philadelphia) | Post-1906 naturalization files; federal court records; Civil War pension files | In-person / NARA catalog online |
| **Diocese of Allentown Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill & Carbon Counties | By request |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Lackawanna & Luzerne Counties | By request |
