| **Chronicling America / Newspapers.com** | Miners' Journal and regional papers | Free (ChronAm) / Subscription (Newspapers.com) |

---

### Quirks & Gotchas — Read Before You Search

1. **Lackawanna County did not exist before 1878.** All Scranton/Carbondale-area records before that date are filed under **Luzerne County** — courts, church registers held at the county level, and deeds alike.
2. **Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration before 1906.** For 1860–1890, church registers and census mortality schedules are the primary vital record substitutes.
3. **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed.** Bridge the gap with 1880 → church records → city directories → naturalization papers → 1900 census.
4. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across three court series** (Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, Orphans' Court) in each county. Search all three; declarations and petitions may be in different courts.
5. **Schuylkill County naturalization volume 007936750 (1849–1915) is 0% indexed** — no name search is possible; it must be browsed image by image.
6. **Church records in this region are bilingual** — Irish Catholic records are in English/Latin, but German Lutheran and Reformed registers appear in the same volumes; note language before concluding a record is or isn't about your family.
7. **Colliery payrolls at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County** may be the only record linking a miner to a specific mine townland or Irish county if no naturalization paper survives.
8. **Molly Maguires trial records and Pinkerton reports** name many Irish miners from Schuylkill, Carbon, and Luzerne Counties — worth checking even for families not implicated, as witnesses and neighbors are named.

> **External links note:** FamilySearch has 2 curated external links for Schuylkill County, both outside the 1860–1890 window (an 1801 tax list and an 1850 census). For the target period, Ancestry's Pennsylvania statewide collections (accessed directly) are the main external resource.

---

### Recommended Search Order for Irish Coal-Region Ancestors

1. **Federal census** 1860, 1870, 1880 — establish the household, birthplaces, and neighbors
2. **Catholic parish registers** — baptisms, marriages, burials (Diocese of Allentown or Scranton archives; FamilySearch browse-only volumes)
3. **Naturalization records** — browse Schuylkill volume 007936750; check all three court series at each county courthouse
4. **Mine accident / coroner records** — if the ancestor died in a mine accident
5. **Passenger lists** — Philadelphia and New York arrivals, using age and year of immigration from census
6. **Molly Maguires and court records** — if your family was in Schuylkill County in the 1860s–1870s
7. **Colliery payrolls** — Historical Society of Schuylkill County (in-person or by correspondence)
8. **Civil War pension files** — NARA, if the miner served 1861–1865
9. **Newspapers** — Miners' Journal for deaths, accidents, and community notices

# Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide
**Period covered:** c. 1749–1791 (colonial grant era through Vermont Republic to statehood)
**FamilySearch Wiki source:** [Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

The territory that became Vermont was genuinely contested by three overlapping authorities during this period, and understanding which authority created a given record is essential before you begin searching.

| Period | Controlling Authority | Record implication |
|---|---|---|
| 1749–1764 | **New Hampshire** (Gov. Benning Wentworth issues NH Grants) | Land charters held in NH; NH grantees named |
| 1764–1777 | **New York** claims jurisdiction; issues competing grants | NY contests NH titles; NY grant records in Albany |
| 1777–1791 | **Vermont Republic** (independent, unrecognized) | VT establishes own courts, towns, probate; records in Montpelier |
| 1791– | **State of Vermont** (14th state, admitted March 4, 1791) | State-level records begin; first federal census 1790 |

**Key boundary note:** Vermont records are organized at the **town level**, not the county level. Land records, vital records, and probate were all handled town-by-town (or in probate districts). Always identify the specific town before searching — a county-only search will miss the primary series.

---

## Record Classes for Pre-Statehood Vermont

### 1. Land and Proprietors' Records ⭐ *Highest-priority source for this period*

This is the richest, most systematic record class for pre-statehood Vermont. Three overlapping sets exist and all three should be searched.

**Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**
Per the FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page, this schedule was prepared under New York colonial authority and enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry records: grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This is explicitly described by FamilySearch as "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state" and predates any Vermont civil registration. This is your most important finding aid for placing a family in Vermont before statehood.

**New Hampshire Wentworth Grants (1749+)**
Governor Benning Wentworth chartered over 130 townships in the Green Mountains. The original charters name the original proprietors (grantees) of each township. These records are held at the **New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management** in Concord, NH. Many have been published in *New Hampshire State Papers* (vol. 25–26) and some are accessible through digital library projects.

**New York Competing Grants**
New York issued its own overlapping patents. If your ancestor held a Yorker title or was caught in the grants controversy, search the **New York State Archives** in Albany. The NY-vs-NH grants conflict generated substantial documentation — court proceedings and surveys — that names individuals on both sides.

**Town Proprietors' Records (post-settlement)**
Once a township was settled, its proprietors held meetings and recorded lot assignments, divisions, and sales. These volumes are held at individual **town clerk offices** or, for some towns, at the **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration** (VSARA) in Montpelier. The FamilySearch wiki notes that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access — these histories are a valuable substitute source.

**Town Clerk Deed Books**
Vermont recorded land deeds at the town level from early settlement. Search the town clerk's office for the specific town. Some early deed books have been microfilmed by FamilySearch; check the **FamilySearch Catalog** under the specific Vermont town name.

**Access:** Vermont State Archives — [https://www.sec.state.vt.us/archives.aspx](https://www.sec.state.vt.us/archives.aspx) | NH Archives — [https://www.sos.nh.gov/archives](https://www.sos.nh.gov/archives) | NY State Archives — [https://www.archives.nysed.gov](https://www.archives.nysed.gov)

---

### 2. Vital Records — Uneven; no statewide registration until 1857

The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki page states explicitly: **statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857**. For the pre-statehood period this means there is no central civil registration to search.

**Town clerk vital records:** The wiki notes that earlier town clerk records "some back to the 1770s, survive unevenly." These are held at individual town offices. Coverage varies town by town — some towns recorded births and marriages consistently; others have gaps. Contact the town clerk directly or check the FamilySearch Catalog for that town.

**Church records:** For the 1750–1791 period, church registers are often the only vital record source. Congregational churches dominated towns settled from Connecticut and Massachusetts (the majority of early Vermont settlers). Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, and Methodist congregations were also present in some towns. Church registers recorded baptisms (in place of births), marriages, and burials. These are held variously at the local church, the denomination's archives, or the Vermont Historical Society. Some have been microfilmed.

**Family bibles and cemetery inscriptions:** For this period, these are primary sources — not supplements. The **Vermont Old Cemetery Association** has transcribed many early cemeteries.

---

### 3. Census Records

**1790 Federal Census** — Vermont was enumerated on August 2, 1790, approximately seven months before statehood (March 4, 1791). Vermont appears in the 1790 federal census as "Vermont." This is indexed and fully searchable on FamilySearch. This is the earliest name-by-name federal list for the territory.

**Tax Lists as Census Substitutes:** No Vermont-specific colonial or Republic-era population census is known for this period. Tax lists (often called "grand lists" in Vermont) serve as the functional substitute, listing heads of household with taxable property. These are held at town offices and VSARA.

**Access:** 1790 census is free and indexed at FamilySearch; Ancestry.com also holds a searchable copy — [https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)

---

### 4. Military Records

Vermont's pre-statehood military history is layered:

- **Before 1777:** Men from the Green Mountains territory served in **New Hampshire and New York provincial/colonial regiments** (and some in Massachusetts units). Search NH and NY military records, not just Vermont ones, for service before the Republic.
- **Green Mountain Boys (1770–1777):** Ethan Allen's militia operated under no formal colonial authority. Some muster records survive at VSARA.
- **Vermont Republic militia (1777–1791):** VSARA holds Vermont-specific Revolutionary War records.
- **Continental Army service:** Many Vermont men served in Continental regiments. **Federal pension files** (bounty-land warrants and pension applications) at NARA are a critical source for any Revolutionary War–era ancestor and often contain the richest biographical data of any record class for this period.

**Access:** NARA — [https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/) | Fold3 (military records, subscription) — [https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/) | VSARA — Montpelier, VT

---

### 5. Probate Records

Vermont organized its probate system into **districts** rather than counties (a Vermont-specific structure). Windsor District was among the earliest established (1781). Probate records — wills, inventories, guardianship files — are held at the **Vermont Probate Court** offices for each district and at VSARA. Pre-statehood probate records from the Vermont Republic period are particularly valuable because they survive when vital records do not.

---

### 6. Court Records

The Vermont Republic established its own courts from 1777 onward. County court records from this era are held at VSARA. These include civil suits (debt, land disputes), criminal cases, and some naturalization-equivalent proceedings. Land-title disputes between NH grantees and Yorker claimants generate substantial pre-statehood court documentation.

---

### 7. Town Histories and Compiled Sources

The FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki specifically flags 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) as a **major research resource**, noting they "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." These histories frequently include: family genealogies contributed by residents, early settler lists drawn from proprietors' records, and cemetery transcriptions. The **Vermont Historical Society** in Montpelier holds a strong collection. Many have been digitized on HathiTrust and Google Books.

---

### 8. Newspapers

Historical newspapers for Vermont in the 1780s–1790s are sparse but exist. The *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington, 1783–1793) is among the earliest. These can contain death notices, legal notices (land sales, probate), and other genealogically useful content.

**Access:** Newspapers.com — [https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/) | also check the Vermont Digital Newspaper Project via the Library of Congress Chronicling America database.

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

Find A Grave holds transcriptions for many Vermont cemeteries — [https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/). For pre-1791 burials, many grave markers no longer survive; consult the Vermont Old Cemetery Association's survey records as a supplement.

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| **Vermont State Archives (VSARA)**, Montpelier | VT Republic records, land records, military, probate, court | [sec.state.vt.us/archives.aspx](https://www.sec.state.vt.us/archives.aspx) |
| **Vermont Historical Society**, Montpelier | Town histories, manuscripts, church records, compiled genealogies | [vermonthistory.org](https://vermonthistory.org) |

| **NARA** (federal) | 1790 census, Revolutionary War pension files, bounty land warrants | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| **FamilySearch** | Microfilmed town/county records; check FamilySearch Catalog by town name | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |

| Record type | Online status |

| 1790 Federal Census | **Indexed + images** — free on FamilySearch |

## Key Quirks and Gotchas

1. **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is your earliest systematic name list** for future-Vermont territory — ~1,800 NH grantees documented under NY authority. It predates any civil registration. *(FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki)*
2. **No statewide civil vital registration until 1857** — town clerk records survive from the 1770s but unevenly. Always go to the individual town, not a state-level index. *(FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki)*
3. **Three competing land-record systems** exist for this period: NH Grants (Concord), NY patents (Albany), and Vermont Republic records (Montpelier). Search all three if a family had land in dispute.
4. **Vermont records at the town level, not county level.** The county is almost never the right unit to search — always identify the specific town first.
5. **For pre-1777 military service, search NH and NY records** — Vermont had no separate military structure before the Republic was declared.
6. **19th-century town histories are a major primary-source proxy** — they reprint proprietors' records and early settler lists not easily found elsewhere. *(FamilySearch Vermont Genealogy wiki)*
7. **Vermont probate uses "districts," not counties** — confirm which district your town of interest fell under before searching.
8. **Connecticut River families (east side of VT) may appear in NH records** — many towns across the river in NH were closely linked to their VT neighbors by family and commerce. Search adjoining Grafton, Sullivan, and Cheshire Counties in NH as well.
9. **Champlain Valley families (west side of VT) may appear in NY records** — check Clinton and Essex Counties in New York for families near Lake Champlain.
